en: Mātṛkā 1 [Legal Procedure]:
When men were solely devoted to the Dharma and were speakers of truth;
At that time, there was no worldly transaction, nor hatred, nor even envy.
When dharma has perished among men, legal procedure (vyavahāra) comes into operation;
and the king is appointed as the observer of legal procedures and the wielder of the rod of punishment.
In this matter, two methods are proclaimed for the purpose of clarifying a disputed point between two litigants: a written document and witnesses. (Narada Smṛti 1.3)
It should be understood as having two characteristics: with superior and without superior.
That which is "with superior" is that in which there is a wager preceded by a formal agreement.
In a dispute involving a wager, whichever of the two parties loses shall be made to pay the wager he himself made, as well as the fine for defeat. (Narada 1.5)
The plaint is declared to be the essence of legal proceedings;
if that is abandoned, the plaintiff loses his case, while he who crosses over it becomes the defendant.
Families, guilds, corporations, and the king as the presiding authority are the foundations of legal proceedings; each subsequent one is more authoritative than the preceding.
It is proclaimed as having four feet, four bases, and four means; it possesses four benefits, pervades four [realms], and accomplishes four tasks.
It has eight limbs, eighteen steps, and likewise a hundred branches;
it has three wombs, two types of application, two gates, and likewise two destinies.
Dharma, legal procedure, custom, and royal edict—
this four-legged judicial process consists of these, each subsequent one superseding the preceding.

In that regard, legal procedure (dharma) is based on truth; judicial practice (vyavahāra), however, rests with witnesses; customary law (caritra) resides in written records; and royal edict (śāsana) lies in the king’s command. (Narada 1.11)
Because he accomplishes [his goals] through the means beginning with conciliation (*sāma*), he is called the "one who employs the four means" (*catuḥsādhana*);
and because he protects the four stages of life (*āśrama*), he is the "one who benefits the four" (*caturhita*).
Because it pervades the doer, the witnesses, the members of the court, and the king itself, part by part, it is therefore remembered as "four-pervading" (caturvyāpin).
Because he accomplishes these four— dharma, material wealth, fame, and likewise the affection of the world— he is proclaimed as the "Accomplisher of the Four."
The king, the officials, the court members, the legal treatise, the astrologer and the scribe, gold, fire, and water— this is declared to be the eightfold constituent of the court.
Recovery of debts, deposits, partnerships, resumption of what was given, and the failure to perform services after having entered into an agreement; Narada 1.16.
Non-payment of wages, as well as sale without ownership, non-delivery after having sold, and likewise rescission after having purchased; Narada 1.17.

The non-performance of agreements, disputes, and matters concerning sons born of the soil; the legal relationship between husband and wife, the partition of inheritance, and then violence. (Narada 1.18)
Likewise, verbal abuse, physical assault, gambling, and miscellaneous matters are declared; thus, it is remembered as having eighteen titles of law.
Another division of these very [actions] is remembered as one hundred and eight;
due to the differences in the activities of human beings, it is said to have a hundred branches. (Nar_M 1.20)
Since it proceeds from these three—desire, anger, and greed—it is proclaimed as having three origins; therefore, this triad is the cause of dispute.
A legal charge (abhiyoga) should be understood as being of two kinds: by suspicion (śaṅkā) and by proof of fact (tattva).
Suspicion arises from association with the wicked, while proof of fact arises from the discovery of stolen goods (hoḍha) and the like. (Nārada 1.22)
Because it is connected with two sides, it is declared to have two doors:
of these two, the first position is the *pūrvapakṣa* (the prima facie argument), and the subsequent one is the counter-position (*pratipakṣa*). (Narada 1.23)
Because it follows both the real and the deceptive, that [speech] is said to be of two kinds:
the real (bhūta) is that which is connected with the true meaning, while the deceptive (chala) is that which is spoken through negligence.
In that regard, a king who seeks to accomplish dharma should tolerate the remaining forms of deception;
he should resort only to what is factual, since prosperity has its root in dharma.
For a self-disciplined king who adjudicates legal cases according to dharma,
seven virtues arise, just as the seven flames of a fire.
Dharma, wealth, fame, the ripening of the world, the winning over of others, great respect from the subjects, and an eternal station in heaven.
Therefore, having attained the seat of dharma, the king, free from envy,
should be impartial toward all beings, upholding the vow of Vaivasvata.
Placing the Dharmaśāstra before him and abiding by the opinion of the presiding judge,
he should examine the legal cases with a concentrated mind in their proper order.

The source of tradition (āgama) must come first, then the subject matter of the legal proceeding (vyavahārapada), followed by the desire for knowledge (vivitsā) and the final decision (nirṇaya); thus, the judicial process (darśana) is fourfold.
Examining the course of legal proceedings with skill, he should guide them according to the path that is not in conflict with the treatises on Dharma and the treatises on worldly affairs (Artha).
Just as a hunter might track the path of a wounded deer by a trace of blood in the undergrowth, so too should one track the path of the Dharma. 1.32.
Where there may be a conflict between the Dharmaśāstra and the Arthaśāstra,
one should set aside what is stated in the Arthaśāstra and practice what is stated in the Dharmaśāstra.
But when there is a conflict with the Dharmaśāstras, even a legal proceeding that is logically sound is weaker than Dharma; by it, Dharma is set aside. (Narada Smṛti 1.34)
For the Blessed Dharma is subtle, beyond the senses, and difficult to investigate;
therefore, one should lead the course of worldly conduct by means of direct perception.
Even one who is not a thief incurs the state of a thief, and a thief attains the state of a non-thief;
through legal proceedings, Māṇḍavya—who was no thief—was treated as a thief.
A legal transaction entered into with women, at night, outside the village, within the house, or with enemies—
even if already concluded— must be performed again.
Because disputes are complex and because even memory may lack reliability,
one who desires to know the truth may, in matters such as debts and the like, allow time to pass as they wish.

In cases of theft of cattle, land, gold, or women; in cases of verbal or physical assault; in urgent matters; in acts of violence; and in cases of false accusation, one should institute a lawsuit immediately.
But he who proceeds with respect to a doubtful matter without having informed the king shall be forcibly punished, and his case shall not succeed.
The plaintiff shall restrain one who does not abide by the matter to be stated or who departs from it,
until the appearance for the summons at the trial.
Confinement may be of four kinds: restricted to a place, limited by time, exile, or [restriction] from work; one who is not confined must not violate such confinement.
In cases such as crossing a river, traversing a wilderness, or encountering danger in an unfavorable region,
one who departs while that prohibition has not yet been fulfilled does not commit an offense.
During the period of legal restraint, if one who is under restraint should violate that restraint, he must be punished;
conversely, if the restrainer acts otherwise, he shall be liable for a fine. (Narada 1.44)

One who desires to settle a debt, one afflicted by disease, one wishing to perform a sacrifice, one beset by calamity, one attacked by another, and likewise one occupied with royal business. (Narada Smṛti 1.45)
Cowherds [should wait] at the time cattle graze; farmers, when the grain is ripening; artisans, at their respective times; and those who bear arms, during a conflict. (Narada Smṛti 1.46)
A messenger who has not yet attained legal capacity, one intent on giving a gift, one observing a vow, and one in a precarious situation must not be detained; nor should the king summon them.

One who has been accused should not accuse another in place of that person without having resolved the matter; nor should one who has been accused by another, or pierced, seek to pierce in return. (Narada Smṛti 1.48)
One should not bring the matter at issue into disarray, nor should one shift to another position; by doing so, one loses the case previously established. (Narada Smṛti 1.49)
One should not bring a false accusation; there is fault for the one who brings a false accusation.
Whatever disciplinary penalty is prescribed in that case shall fall upon the accuser.
Making excuses while wasting time, speaking in the assembly,
and speaking after having already said what was to be said— these are the characteristics of one who is losing ground.
He who flees when summoned, or who does not engage in a lawsuit when it has been brought before him,
shall be punished by the king and indeed be deprived of his case.
In legal proceedings that have been concluded, even documentary evidence or witnesses become fruitless if they were not previously presented. (Narada 1.53)
Just as the qualities of the rainy season are fruitless when the grains have already ripened,
so too is authoritative proof useless for those whose legal case has already been decided.
Even that which is untrue, if spoken at the appropriate time, is examined;
but that which is not spoken due to negligence is lost, even if it be true. (Narada Smṛti 1.55)
If one should consider that a case has been decided or adjudicated contrary to the law,
he shall impose double the fine and reopen that matter.
But if the legal proceeding is wrongly judged, the members of the court shall incur that same punishment;
for indeed, no one ever remains on the path of righteousness without the threat of punishment. (Narada 1.57)
If anyone, out of passion, ignorance, or even greed, should speak otherwise [than the truth], he should be known as an unseemly member of the assembly; the king should severely punish him.
However, by a king who especially desires to protect his own duty, the goodness or wickedness [of others] must be examined due to the diversity of human minds. (Narada Smriti 1.59)
There are men who, out of greed, would give false testimony;
and there are others, evil-minded people, who forge fraudulent documents.
Therefore, the king must especially examine both of these:
a written document according to the rules for writing, and witnesses according to the rules for witnesses. (Narada 1.61)
Unreal things appear as if real, and real things appear as if unreal;
various phenomena are seen in this way, therefore investigation is appropriate. (Nar_M 1.62)
The sky appears as level as a palm, and the firefly like a flame;
yet there is no level surface in the sky, nor is there fire in the firefly.
Therefore, even an object perceived by direct perception ought to be examined;
one who makes known objects after having examined them does not fall away from dharma.
Seeing thus, the king who always remains composed while conducting legal affairs spreads his radiant fame here and attains the realm of the Sun.

Mātṛkā 2 (Mātṛkā 2 is found only in manuscript P. [The second chapter of the Mātṛkā included in Jolly’s edition and translation does not belong to the original *Nāradasmṛti* (see the Introduction to the text).]
[The translation is provided in the Appendix.
[In the vernacular:
One who has gained firm confidence, being desirous and impelled by his own purpose, [should proceed].
But having reached a definitive conclusion regarding the matter at hand, he should cause the plaintiff's case to be recorded in writing.
But the defendant, having heard the meaning of the plaintiff's case, should immediately thereafter present his counter-argument connected to the subject matter of that case. (Narada 2.2)
He who desires [to contest] may obtain a written document the next day, or after three days, or even after seven days;
however, one who is fit for the third quarter of the case is certainly a winner immediately.
The reply (uttara) may be of four kinds: a false admission, a counter-claim, an admission of a prior judgment, or a plea based on a legal procedure already completed. (Narada 2.4)
"This is false; I do not know it, for I was not present there at that time, and I was not yet born then—thus, falsehood is of four kinds."
The rejoinder may be of four kinds: false, contradictory, involving the addition of words, and connected with the meaning of the opponent's prior position. (Narada 2.6)

The plaintiff shall cause the matter to be written down as long as the defendant has not yet entered his answer; this shall continue until the entire subject matter intended to be expressed has been set forth.

A document that has a different purpose, lacks substance, is devoid of authoritative sources or tradition, contains omissions or additions, or is corrupted—these are declared to be defects of the composition. (Narada 2.8)
Whatever is to be obtained by whom, from whatever source, that he shall obtain from that;
for one thing does not come from another, nor does one thing come from something else—thus this [teaching] is threefold for the sake of others.
I too have been meditated upon here by your friend with a mind like that of an enemy;
therefore, it was for the sake of great patience that you were thus informed by me.
That which is deficient in substance, devoid of the basis for the fruit,
and lacking in legal authority— one should discard such a document as being defective in its writing.
In the first chapter, one should avoid a fault that is devoid of scriptural authority,
as well as a conflict between one person and many, or between a city and a kingdom.
If there be a deficiency or excess of bindus, mātrās, words, or syllables due to a single error in the rule, it becomes useless; one should avoid such [a recitation] with effort.
Furthermore, one should clearly avoid even that which is corrupted, poorly situated, or ruined by water, oil, and the like; such speech is not clear and its meaning is indistinct. (Nar_M 2.14)
Even if a statement is established, it does not constitute truth if it deviates from external, conventional reality. (Nar_M 2.15)
That was offered by me while I was staying on Mount Gandhamādana;
this is external to the dharma of worldly convention and is not established as valid.
By the insertion of other syllables and by the shifting to another meaning,
the gift of action becomes confused, and the action itself becomes confused.
Whatever [objection] one might state regarding the instrument when provoked by passion and so forth, all of that should first be written by the proponent on a board or similar surface. (Nar_M2.18)
For the sake of unconfused understanding, those established in the Dharma have thoroughly investigated this;
therefore, the proponent must exclude anything other than that, such as the fruit and so forth, from the examples.
Permitted by the two disputants, they shall record the remainder of the case as it stands on the writing-board, along with the witnesses and the admission of the two litigants.

Whatever remains after what has been written by the two disputants, and which is subsequently remembered by the disputant, is called *pratyākalita*; it is recorded at its own place [in the record]. (Narada 2.21)
Whether commissioned by the plaintiff or sent by the defendant, whoever litigates on behalf of another, victory and defeat belong to those two [parties]. (Narada Smṛti 2.22)
He who is neither a brother, nor a father, nor a son, nor one acting under a commission,
yet speaks for the sake of another and gives false testimony even in a legal proceeding, shall be punished.
He who abandons his original thesis and takes up another again should be known as a person of inferior argumentation, due to shifting his position in debate.

In all disputes, one does not lose the case through verbal quibble; however, in matters concerning cattle, women, land, or the non-payment of debt, even if one is punished, one does not lose the substance of the claim.
If the defendant,
when charged, should deny the charge, the plaintiff must prove the case, provided that he has not been discredited by a counter-claim.
For whatever has been written in the first part, letter by letter and in its entirety,
the plaintiff shall establish that same matter through evidence in the third part.
Action is also said to be of two kinds: human and likewise divine.
Human action is known through documents and witnesses; that which consists of the balance-scale and other such means is declared to be divine.
When a legal procedure has been conducted during the day in villages or cities,
and witnesses are available, a divine ordeal is not to be employed as a means of proof.
In a forest, in a deserted place, at night, inside a house,
in cases of violence, and likewise in the denial of a deposit, the ordeal by divine means is applicable.

When the prima facie case has been contradicted by the presentation of the grounds [for the opposing view], the defendant must indeed act with diligence; it should be understood as being like the prima facie case itself.
One who flees when summoned, one who remains silent, one defeated by the witnesses, and one who confesses of his own accord— these are the four kinds of defeated litigants.

One who speaks otherwise, one who hates the performance of the legal act, one who does not appear, one who is unable to provide an answer, and one who flees when summoned— these five are recorded as being defeated.
Gems such as rubies, gold coins and the like, pearls, coral, conch shells, and so forth, when stolen, go to the owner if they are of high quality. (Narada Smṛti 2.34)
But regarding perfumes, garlands, ornaments, or even clothing that has not been given—[the king] has declared that one who steps upon such things, or sandals, deserves death. (Nar.M 2.35)
The price of merchandise, wages, a deposit, a fine, and whatever is paid as a legal fee,
as well as gifts made in vain, stakes at dice, and gambling bets— these do not increase [with interest] unless they are intended to do so.
Those of Śūdra birth who bring false accusations against the twice-born,
the king shall have their tongues cut out and impaled upon a stake.

Whether it be an edict, a letter, a patent, a royal decree, a mortgage deed, a sale, or a purchase, those who know the law should recognize as the plaintiff (pūrvapakṣa) the one who first makes a formal complaint to the king. (Narada 2.38)
When the witnesses are accused, the purification of the previous witnesses must first be carried out;
once those witnesses have been cleared, one may thereafter purify the testimony.

If witnesses, assessors, or judges are found to be corrupt, there is a rule for a retrial; however, for those who have reached a conclusion through their own conduct, there is no provision for a second trial.
Even if he has admitted his own guilt, even if he is exhausted by his own conduct,
and even if he has failed in his actions, he deserves the final judgment of the assembly.
Having set aside the arguments, the members of the court must reach a definitive decision on the matter;
for if a case is decided without setting aside the arguments, there will be conflict both in this world and after death.
If he is defeated by the assessors themselves, he shall later be punished by the king according to his own legal code;
and the victor should also be granted a formal document of victory as is proper.
This gateway to legal procedure was previously declared by the Self-Existent One;
for when the gateway is pure, there shall be purity of the legal process, and not otherwise. (Narada Smṛti 2.44)
But the one appointed to the assembly (mātṛkā) must speak words that are free from partiality. (Nar_M3.1)
A member of the court who speaks what is appropriate shall incur neither hatred nor guilt;
but a member of the court who speaks otherwise shall incur both of those.
The king, however, should appoint righteous assessors who have been well-tested and who are capable of bearing the burden of legal proceedings, like excellent oxen. (Narada Smṛti 3.3)
The members of the king's assembly should be well-versed in the meaning of the treatises on Dharma, of noble birth, speakers of truth, and impartial toward both enemy and friend. (Narada Smṛti 3.4)
Dharma is known to be established upon that [the king], and the king is the root of Dharma;
therefore, O King, the monarch should purify legal proceedings in consultation with the virtuous.
In pure legal proceedings, the members of the court attain purity;
for their purity comes from dharma, therefore they should speak only dharma.
Where righteousness is slain by unrighteousness, and truth by falsehood,
while the members of the assembly look on, there the members of the assembly themselves are slain.
For when Dharma, pierced by Adharma, approaches the assembly, if it is not extracted as the arrow, then the members of that assembly are themselves pierced. (Narada Smṛti 3.8)
Either one should not enter an assembly, or one should speak what is just;
for a man who remains silent or speaks falsely becomes a sinner.
But those members of the assembly who, having entered the court, sit silently lost in thought and do not speak as is required—all of them are speakers of falsehood. (Narada Smṛti 3.10)
One quarter of the unrighteousness falls upon the perpetrator, one quarter reaches the witness,
one quarter reaches all the members of the court, and one quarter reaches the king.
The king becomes [sinless], and the members of the assembly are released from guilt;
the sin goes to the perpetrator where one deserving of censure is censured. (Narada Smṛti 3.12)
He who, having entered the assembly, speaks behind one's back due to a deficiency of wealth, eats like a blind man who disregards the fish along with their thorns.
Therefore, having entered an assembly, a member of that assembly, free from passion and hatred,
should speak such words as would not cause him to fall into hell.
Just as a learned physician extracts a splinter by means of an instrument,
so too should the judge extract the "splinter" [of injustice] through legal procedure.
Where all the members of the assembly consider, "This is well done," that dispute shall be free from thorns; otherwise, it shall be thorny.
That is no assembly where there are no elders; they are no elders who do not speak the Dharma.
That is no Dharma where there is no truth; that is no truth which is pierced by deceit.
The titles of legal procedure (vyavahārapada):
1. Non-payment of debt (ṛṇādāna).
Debt is that which is to be given and that which is not to be given; by whom, where, and in what manner it is to be paid; and what [the debt is].
And from the law concerning the giving and receiving [of gifts], the non-payment of debts is traditionally known as the first head of dispute.
When the father has passed away, the sons shall pay the debt according to their respective shares, whether they are divided or undivided, provided that he who bears that burden [pays]. (Narada 1.02)
Whatever debt has been contracted by an undivided paternal uncle, or by a brother, or by a mother for the sake of the family, the heirs shall pay that entire amount. (Narada 1.03)
The debt that was cleared by sons, which they inherited in succession without obstruction, must be paid by grandsons; it ceases with the fourth generation.
For this reason, fathers desire sons from whatever cause it may be, thinking:
"He will liberate me from my creditors. (Nar_1.05)
Therefore, once a son is born, he should strive with effort to liberate his father from debt so that he does not fall into hell, even at the cost of sacrificing his own interests.
If an ascetic who maintains the sacred fires dies while still burdened by debt, both his asceticism and his fire-sacrifices become the wealth of his creditors. 1.07.

A father shall not pay a debt contracted by his son, but a son may pay one contracted by his father, except for debts incurred through lust, anger, liquor, gambling, or acting as a surety. (Narada 1.08)
Whatever debt was incurred at the father’s own command, or for the sake of maintaining the family, or contracted during a time of distress— that the father shall repay to the son.
Whatever has been set aside for the sake of the family by disciples, resident pupils, servants, wives, and attendants, that must be carried by the head of the household. (Nar_1.10)
If the father has gone abroad, the son shall not pay the debt before twenty years have passed, nor to a paternal uncle, nor even to an elder brother. (Narada 1.11)
Even if he is alone, he must pay the debt contracted by those authorized while he was alive; but when they have died, his son is not required to pay that debt to others.
A woman shall not pay a debt contracted by her husband, nor likewise one contracted by her son,
except for what she has herself promised or what was contracted jointly with her husband.
A childless widow who has been authorized by her husband, or one who is about to die, should give [the debt];
or he who takes her inheritance, for from the inheritance comes the debt. (Narada 1.14)

And a debt incurred by a wife shall not in any way become the husband's obligation, except for what was contracted during times of distress; for the expansion of the household depends upon the men. (Narada 1.15)
Except for the wives of washermen, hunters, cowherds, and liquor-sellers;
their livelihood depends on them, and their families rely upon them. (Nar_1.16)
But a woman who, having sons, abandons her own son and resorts to another man, shall have all her property taken away; for the son alone shall take the entire estate of a woman who is destitute.
But if a woman who is accompanied by her dowry and has offspring should resort to another man,
he shall pay her husband's debt or she may likewise abandon him.
For when a man dies without wealth and without a son, whoever takes his wife incurs the burden of his debts; that [wife] alone is traditionally considered his property.
Among those who take away wealth, a wife, or sons, he who takes the wealth shall bear the debt;
if both the wife and the wealth are absent, the one who takes the wife bears it; and if both the wealth and the son are absent, the one who takes the wealth bears it.
The woman who is independent (svairiṇī) is the most excellent among those who have remarried;
he who marries either of these two must pay the debt incurred by her husband.
They say that transactions performed by a woman are invalid when not in times of distress, especially those involving the giving, mortgaging, or selling of a house or field. (Narada 1.22)
These authorities also apply if the husband gives his consent;
or, in the absence of the husband, the son; or, in the absence of both husband and son, the king. (Narada 1.23)
Whatever has been given by a gratified husband to his wife, she may enjoy or give away at her pleasure even after he has died, with the exception of immovable property.
Likewise, a task performed by a servant is declared to be unperformed, except when commanded by the master; for a servant has no authority over himself. (Nar_1.25)
If a son performs a service that his father does not desire, it is said to be as if it were never done at all; for a slave and a son are considered equal in this regard.
For even one who is independent is not liable for debt if he has not attained legal capacity;
independence, however, is traditionally held to belong to the eldest, based on seniority produced by qualities and age. (Narada 1.27)
In this world, there are three who are independent: the king, the teacher, and likewise the householder in his own home for each and every member of the castes. (Nar_1.28)
All subjects are dependent, while the lord of the earth is independent;
the disciple is traditionally held to be dependent, whereas the teacher possesses independence. (Nar_1.29)
Wives, sons, and slaves, along with all property, are not independent;
rather, the householder is independent therein, for whatever belongs to him has come down through his lineage.
One who is in the womb until the eighth year should be known as a child (śiśu);
one up to sixteen years is known as a boy (bāla), and is also designated as a youth (pogaṇḍa). (Nar_1.31)
One who knows legal procedure is independent of others, except for his parents;
while they live, he remains dependent even if he is advanced in age.
Of these two as well, the father is superior, because the primacy of the seed is observed;
in the absence of the progenitor, the mother [is superior], and in her absence, the elder brother.
All these [members of the family] are always independent in relation to those who are dependent;
they are considered masters in matters of instruction, distribution, and sale. (Nar_1.34)
Whatever action a child performs, and likewise one who is not independent, those people learned in the scriptures declare that such an act is as if unperformed. (Nar_1.35)

For even that effect which one who is independent might produce when not subject to external conditions, they say is as good as unproduced; he is not independent because of his dependence on causes. (Nar_1.36)
Those who are afflicted by lust and anger, distressed by fear and calamity,
and overwhelmed by passion and hatred, should be known as having fallen into an unnatural state.

Whatever is performed by the eldest, the most excellent, and one who is established in his natural state within the family, that deed is truly done; what is done by one who is not independent is not considered done.
All activities have wealth as their root; therefore, effort is considered necessary for its acquisition.
Its method is, in due order: protection, increase, and enjoyment. (Nar_1.39)
Furthermore, that [conduct] should be known as threefold: white, variegated, and indeed black; its seven distinct divisions should be understood separately. (Nar_1.40)

Wealth acquired through learning, heroism, austerity, daughters, disciples, sacrificial clients, and inheritance—this sevenfold wealth is "white" (pure), and its increase is likewise of that same nature. (Nar_1.41)
That which is acquired through idleness, agriculture, trade, tolls, the practice of crafts, or as a favor from one who has rendered assistance, is declared to be "spotted" (śabala). 1.42.
That which is acquired through gambling, serving as a messenger, distress, hypocrisy, violence, or by means of a pretext is declared to be "black" (kṛṣṇa). (Nar_1.43)
By means of that, buying and selling, giving and taking, as well as various activities and even the enjoyment of wealth, proceed. (Nar_1.44)
Whatever a person performs with whatever kind of material substance, he obtains a corresponding fruit both in this world and after death. (Nar_1.45)
Furthermore, that [mindfulness] is said to be of twelve kinds based on its respective objects;
it is threefold as common, while the remainder is said to be ninefold.
Inherited property, a gift of affection, and what is acquired together with one's wife—
these are the three kinds of wealth for all castes without distinction.

The specific wealth of a Brāhmaṇa should be known as having three characteristics: that which is obtained through receiving gifts, from a patron for whom one performs sacrifices, and likewise from a pupil. 1.48.
They say that for a Kṣatriya as well, there are three specific kinds of wealth: what is acquired in battle, taxes, and fines resulting from legal proceedings. (Nar_1.49)

The specific wealth of a Vaiśya should also be known as having three characteristics: agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade; while that of a Śūdra consists of service to these [higher castes]. (Narada Smṛti 1.50)
This is the righteous way for all castes to acquire wealth;
by the opposite method it would be unrighteous, unless there is a grave emergency.
In times of distress, the conduct of a Vaiśya is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa as the next best alternative; it is never declared to be inferior to that.
A Brahmin should never perform the work of a Shudra, nor should a Shudra perform the work of a Brahmin; for those two [tasks] lead to their downfall.
Between those two, no superior or inferior action exists;
for, having abandoned intermediate actions, they are indeed common to all.
Having crossed over his distress by means of wealth acquired through the occupation of a Kṣatriya,
the Brāhmaṇa should relinquish that Kṣatriya occupation once he has performed purification for himself.
But that Brāhmaṇa who, out of passion, delights in that very [low] occupation is fallen from the path; he is proclaimed as a *kāṇḍapṛṣṭha*, unfit to sit in the row for meals.
In the occupation of a Vaiśya, the following are not to be sold by a Brāhmaṇa: milk, curd, ghee, honey, beeswax, lac, alkali, juice, and spirituous liquor.
Meat, boiled rice, sesame, linen, Soma, flowers, fruits, leaves, humans, poison, weapons, water, salt, cakes, and creepers; Nar_1.58 //
Indigo, silk, skins, bones, blankets made of goat hair, and one-hoofed animals; likewise, clay, buttermilk, hair, oil-cakes, vegetables, and medicinal herbs. *Narasiṃha Purāṇa* 1.59.
However, for a Brāhmaṇa, dry wood and grass may be sold,
with the exception of fragrant substances, *arakāva*, *itra*, cotton, roots, and chaff.
And he may use wood that has fallen of its own accord, as well as split bamboo, fruits of the jujube and *iṅguda* trees,
and a rope made of cotton thread, provided that it remains unaltered.
In the event of incapacity for the sake of medicine, and likewise for the purpose of a sacrifice,
sesame seeds may indeed be sold, provided they are exchanged for an equal amount of grain.
A Brahmin who sells items that ought not to be sold has fallen from the path;
he must be restored to the path by the king with a severe punishment. (Nar_1.63)
The means of valid cognition must be diligently protected by those who abide by the means of valid cognition;
for the means of valid cognition fail when they are not themselves properly established.
A written document, witnesses, and possession are declared to be the threefold proof by which the owner enjoys his wealth upon its acquisition. (Narada 1.65)

A written document is always powerful, while witnesses are effective only as long as they live; through the lapse of time, possession prevails—this is the settled conclusion in the scriptures. (Narada 1.66)
Among these three types of perceived means of valid cognition, each preceding one should be known as more authoritative than the following; of these, direct experience is the most authoritative.
Even when a written document exists and witnesses are still living, that which has not been enjoyed—especially in the case of immovable property—is not secure. (Narada 1.68)
He who, out of folly, neglects his own wealth while it is being enjoyed by others—
even while he himself is alive— his very enjoyment of it brings that wealth under their control.
Whatever property an owner observes being enjoyed by others for ten years while remaining silent in their presence, he does not deserve to recover it.
If he remains silent and indifferent while this time previously mentioned passes by, his legal claim shall not be established. (Narada 1.71)
If the owner is not an idiot and is not a minor, and his property is enjoyed by another, that enjoyment is established by legal usage; the enjoyer is entitled to that wealth.

A pledge, a boundary, the property of a minor, an open deposit, a sealed deposit, women, royal property, and the property of one learned in the Vedas are not lost through adverse possession. (Narada 1.73)
Through direct enjoyment, twenty years of a master’s ownership cause even items such as deposits to be lost, with the exception of the property of a wife or a king. (Narada 1.74)
And the property of women and of kings is never lost by prescription, even if it is enjoyed for hundreds of years without a legal title. (Nar_1.75)
Where enjoyment is observed but no tradition (āgama) is seen anywhere, there the tradition is the cause; enjoyment is not the cause in that case. (Nar_1.76)
That which is enjoyed without having been acquired does not transcend the nature of mere enjoyment;
however, when the enjoyer has passed away, that wealth becomes the property to be enjoyed by his descendants.
One who is accused as a taker of property should produce documentary evidence;
for those acquired from one's father in due succession, possession alone shall constitute proof of ownership.
That which is deposited, that which is taken away, that which is left behind, that which is seized by force, that which is borrowed,
and that which is enjoyed in one's absence— these six are [lost] without a legal title.
When a deceased litigant has thus engaged in a dispute, his son must settle that matter; possession does not override it.
Even without scriptural authority, that which has been enjoyed by the three preceding ancestors cannot be overturned, having been transmitted through three generations in due order. (Nar_1.81)
Even those who are virtuous would not be valid witnesses after the death of the wealthy man,
except for what was previously declared by him when he himself was near death.
For when the defendant is dead, the testimony of witnesses is not the means of proof;
in that case, the instrument possessing witnesses would be the means for reaching a definitive conclusion.

Even if it is merely reported by a sick person, whatever matter connected with dharma has been stated, one may be a witness to that even after [the person] has died; this applies as well in the case of the six types of deposits, such as those entrusted for delivery.
Among all debts and the like, each subsequent one is more powerful;
among those concerning the acceptance of gifts, each preceding one is weightier.
For the acceptance of gifts is intended for the purpose of obtaining a place [of residence];
that is declared to be usury, and by means of it is the livelihood of usurers. (Nar_1.86)
In the treatises, its interest is recorded as being fourfold: bodily, periodic, stipulated, and likewise compound interest known as *cakravṛddhi*. Nar_1.87.
That which does not conflict with one's physical well-being and is paid as a fixed fee is bodily interest;
that increase which flows month by month is known as periodical interest. (Nar_1.88)
Interest that is stipulated by the debtor himself is called "stipulated interest" (kāritā);
interest upon interest is declared to be "compound interest" (cakravṛddhi). (Nar_1.89)
This rule for increasing interest is declared to be universally applicable;
however, there is another rule according to local custom where a debt remains outstanding.
In one region it remains double, in another triple, and likewise in yet another fourfold;
thus, in various regions, it exists as eightfold.
The interest on gold, grain, and clothing is two, three, and fourfold respectively;
the interest on ghee is eightfold, and for women and cattle, it is offspring.
Of cotton thread, cotton, and fermenting agents; of gourds and lead; of all weapons; and of leather, copper, and iron.
And for all other bricks as well,
Prajāpati Manu has declared that their increase is inexhaustible.
The increase for all types of oils, liquors, honey, and clarified butter,
as well as for molasses and salt, should be known to be eightfold.
Interest on gifts given out of affection shall never accrue if not requested;
however, even if unrequested, it increases after half a year has passed.
This rule for interest has been declared according to dharma for one who lends at interest; however, that interest which is prescribed for grains is designated as usury (vārdhuṣya). || 1.97 ||
A Vaiśya may indeed overcome distress through the practice of usury at his will;
however, even in the most dire calamities, a Brāhmaṇa must never engage in usury.
If there is no one of the same lineage to whom the Brahmin's inheritance should be given, one should offer it to a kinsman of his;
in his absence, to his relatives.
But when there are no kinsmen, nor relatives or blood relations, then one should give it to those of one's own caste; if none of these exist, one should cast it into the water. (Narada 1.100)
The creditor shall deliver the principal with interest to the debtor who has come to collect it;
but if he refuses when requested, he shall incur the loss of the remainder.
When the debt has been cleared, he should deliver a written document; in its absence, a verbal acknowledgment.
In this way, there shall be mutual clearance between the creditor and the debtor. (Narada 1.102)
In this matter, there are two causes for confidence: a surety and a pledge;
and two means of proof that bring clarity: a written document and witnesses. (Narada 1.103)
For attendance, for giving, and likewise for providing assistance—the wise have observed three kinds of sureties for these three purposes alone. (Nar_1.104)
If debtors fail to repay or if the matter is disputed at the time of payment, the guarantor shall pay that debt; likewise, he shall pay it if they fail to appear.
If there are many sureties, they shall pay the debt as agreed;
for when the specific amount is not specified among them, the payment is made according to the will of the creditor.
Whatever debt a surety may pay when pressured by the creditor,
the debtor shall reimburse that amount to the surety twofold.
That which is pledged is known as *ādhi*; it should be understood as being of two kinds:
that for which a time limit has been set and brought forward, and likewise that which remains until the debt is repaid. (Narada 1.108)
Furthermore, it is said to be of two kinds: that which is to be guarded and likewise that which is to be enjoyed;
likewise, its restitution, as well as gain and loss in the reverse case.
Similarly, if through negligence the pledge of a wealthy person undergoes deterioration or is destroyed—except in cases caused by fate or the king—the principal shall be lost. (Narada 1.110)
If a pledge, even when being carefully guarded, should become worthless with the passage of time,
another pledge must be provided, or the debt must be paid to the creditor.
Now, if he should become devoid of resources due to the reversal of time and remains a debtor,
he shall be made to pay the debt as it becomes possible, at the appropriate times according to his income.
If, despite being capable, one does not repay the debt to the creditor due to wickedness,
he shall be compelled by the king to pay it, after the king has taken a twentieth part as a fine.
If the amount of a debt owed by a debtor should be lost here over time,
the recovery of the [debtor's] caste, name, and residence is declared to depend upon the written document.

A document should be known to be of two kinds: that written by one's own hand and that written by another; likewise, it may be without witnesses or with witnesses. The validity of these two depends upon their established usage in the region.
A document that is not contrary to local customs, which clearly identifies the parties involved, and whose sequence and letters are uncorrupted, is recognized as valid evidence. (Narada 1.116)
That which is done by one intoxicated, or by a woman or a child, or through force;
likewise, that which is done out of fear or under duress is rendered invalid. (Narada 1.117)
Where the witnesses, the creditor, the debtor, and the scribe have all died, that document is also invalid, except in the case of a mortgage which serves as a stable basis of proof. (Narada 1.118)
The pledge (ādhi) is said to be of two kinds: movable and immovable;
in this matter, the realization [of ownership] for both occurs only if there is possession, and not otherwise.

A document that has been presented at the proper time, and whatever has been proclaimed or caused to be proclaimed, is established as valid everywhere, even when the witnesses have died. (Narada 1.120)
A document that has not been heard of, not seen, or exists merely for the sake of legal procedure does not attain validity, even while witnesses are still living. (Narada 1.121)
When a document has been deposited in another country, burnt, poorly written, or stolen, there shall be a determination of its validity at that time;
if it does not exist, proof must be seen through witnesses.

Whenever there may be doubt regarding a document concerning facts, whether true or false, one should resolve it by means of the signature of the party's own hand, identifying marks, possession, and logical reasoning. 1.123.
Any document that bears another's name or was produced for some other purpose must,
in case of dispute, be examined by means of its internal consistency, the circumstances of its acquisition, and the underlying motives.

Any document that bears another's name or was produced for some other purpose must be examined when there is a dispute, by means of [evidence regarding] its connection and the circumstances of its acquisition.
A document should be contested by means of another document, and witnesses by means of witnesses;
however, a document is superior to witnesses, and witnesses are inferior to a document. (Narada 1.125)
In cases where a document is torn, broken, stolen, wiped out, lost, or poorly written, another document must be executed; this is recorded as the rule for documents. (Narada 1.126)
But when matters are in doubt and two parties are disputing, the clarification of the truth is seen to depend upon witnesses, because they have seen, heard, or experienced [the events]. (Nar_1.127)
A witness is to be understood as one who has seen with both ears and eyes;
that which another says is for the ear, and that which is bodily action is for the eye. (Nar_1.128)
That witness is seen by the wise to be of eleven kinds;
among them, five are said to be appointed and six are said to be unappointed.
The written witness, the reminded witness, the incidental witness, the secret witness, and the corroborating witness—thus the witness is declared to be of five kinds. (Narada 1.130)
The wise have also proclaimed that the judicial process is sixfold,
consisting of the village assembly, the presiding judge, and the king for the litigants.
Those who are insiders in legal affairs, those sent by a litigant, and those from the same family in disputes between families—these too may be witnesses. (Narada 1.132)
Those who are of noble birth, upright, pure by birth, by action, and by wealth;
at least three in number, blameless, pure, and possessed of sound intellect—such persons shall be witnesses. (Narada 1.133)
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, as well as those who are blameless— these may belong to each respective caste, or alternatively, they may all belong to all castes.
In guilds, the members of the guild; in their own groups, the group members; among outsiders, the outsiders; and among women, women shall be witnesses. (Narada 1.135)
But if someone within groups such as guilds should become an object of hatred, he must not be a witness for those very same people, for they would all be his haters. (Narada 1.136)
For even one who is not a witness is seen by the wise in the treatises to be of five kinds:
[the false witness] due to speech, due to fault, due to division, due to self-accusation, and the deceased intermediary.

Where witnesses are divided in a legal dispute— some being learned Vedic scholars based on their testimony, others being thieves and the like based on the observation of their faults— there shall be a conflict of opinions.

One who, having not been designated by the party himself, comes of his own accord and speaks, is considered a "dead man" (mṛtāntara), except in the case of one who was made aware of the claim while the claimant was dying. (Narada 1.139)
Vedic scholars, ascetics, the elderly, and those men who have renounced the world are not witnesses; no reason for this has been stated here.
Thieves, violent criminals, the fierce, gamblers, and likewise executioners—these are not witnesses because of their wickedness; truth is not found in them. (Nar_1.141)
When witnesses have been accepted by the king for the determination of a single matter,
if their statements diverge, they shall be considered non-witnesses due to that disagreement.
But he who, not being appointed as a witness, comes of his own accord and speaks, is called a "sūcī" (informant) in the scriptures; he does not deserve the status of a witness.
If there were no matter to be communicated, nor a petitioner for whom it should be told, where could one exercise witnesshood? Thus, one who dies in the interval is not a witness. (Narada 1.144)
If there were no matter to be communicated, nor anyone to request it, where could that person exercise witness-hood? Thus, one who dies in the interval is not a witness. (Narada 1.144)
When two parties are disputing over a matter and there are witnesses for both,
those witnesses shall belong to the one whose case is the first to be presented.
In whatever matter the weakness of the plaintiff's case arises by virtue of his own conduct, the witnesses of the defendant must be questioned in that dispute. (Narada 1.146)
One should not approach a witness in private at the instigation of another;
nor should one cause a rift between them and others. By acting in this manner, one shall certainly suffer loss.
If the witness designated should die or depart to another region, those who heard him shall be the authority; for the subsequent action is the authority.

Even after a very long time, that which has been written shall attain its fulfillment; one who knows [the procedure] should write it himself, but one who does not know should have it written by another. (Nar_1.149)
Success is declared here for a witness who is reminded after eight years;
likewise, success is achieved for one who appears spontaneously within five years. (Narada 1.150)
Success for a secret witness is attained within three years;
for a subsequent witness, they say success is achieved within one year. (Narada 1.151)
Alternatively, no fixed time limit has been observed regarding a witness;
for those learned in the scriptures say that the status of a witness depends upon memory. (Narada 1.152)
That man whose memory and hearing have not been impaired,
even over a very long period of time, is fit to serve as a witness to testimony.
But other six types of disputes are declared to be those where there is no reliance on witnesses;
the wise say that for these, the very characteristics [of the case] constitute witnesshood.
One with a firebrand in hand should be known as an arsonist; one with a weapon in hand is a murderer; and one seized by the hair of the head is a simultaneous adulterer. 1.155.
One who approaches with a spade in hand should be known as a destroyer of the dam;
likewise, one with an axe in hand is proclaimed to be a cutter of the forest. (Nar_1.156)
A man who commits physical assault is to be recognized by prominent marks [on his body];
for these matters of assault are not dependent on witnesses, but rather require close investigation. (Nar_1.157)
Someone, having marked themselves with a sign, might out of malice cause harm to another;
in such a case, an investigation is appropriate by means of the logical grounds, the purpose, and the capacity of the situation. (Nar_1.158)
Those who have a personal interest in the matter, those who are not trustworthy, those who are allies, or those who are enemies;
those whose faults are known, those afflicted by disease, or those who are corrupted—these should not be questioned. (Nar_1.159)
Slaves, those who act with deceit, the faithless, the elderly, women, children, and wheel-turners (heretics);
the intoxicated, the insane, the heedless, the afflicted, gamblers, and village priests; Nar_1.160.

Long-distance travelers, sea-faring merchants, those who have renounced the world, the sick, hunters, Vedic scholars, those lacking proper conduct, eunuchs, and those of immoral character. // Nar_1.161 //

Those who are nihilists, those who have abandoned their wives and the sacred fire, those who officiate at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice, those who eat from a single vessel, those who associate with enemies, and those who are kinsmen by birth; // Nar_1.162 //
Actors who have previously been seen to commit faults, poisoners, snake-charmers, those who administer poison,
arsonists, usurers, the sons of Śūdra women, and those born of illicit unions— [these are to be avoided].
Those exhausted by reckless acts, the weary, the destitute, and the outcastes;
those of broken conduct, those who have not returned from their studies, the dull-witted, oil-pressers, and root-diggers.

Those possessed by spirits, those hostile to kings, those who predict rain or the positions of the stars, those who proclaim misfortune, those who sell themselves, and those whose livelihood depends on the private parts of women; Nar_1.165 //

One with deformed nails, one with a dark-complexioned face, one afflicted with leucoderma, a betrayer of friends, a rogue, a vintner, a magician, a hunter, a cruel man, and those who oppose guilds or corporations; Nar_1.166 //
A murderer, a painter, a wandering performer, one who has fallen from his caste, a forger, a cheat, a debtor, a thief, and a royal officer; 1.167.
One who sells human beings, poison, weapons, water, salt, cakes, or climbing plants; a Brāhmaṇa who is a usurer; and any twice-born man who is a moneylender.
One who has fallen from his own duty, a member of a guild, a panegyrist, a servant of the lowly,
one who disputes with his father, and a sower of discord— these are non-witnesses.
Even those who have been designated as non-witnesses, such as slaves, dishonest persons, and others,
may become witnesses when the gravity of the case requires it.
In all cases of violence, theft,
adultery, and both forms of harsh speech, one should not examine the witnesses.
Among them, neither a child, nor one who is alone, nor a woman, nor a deceitful person, nor a kinsman, nor an enemy shall give false testimony. (Narada 1.172)
A fool may speak falsely out of ignorance; a woman, out of a habit of wickedness; a forger, out of deceit; a kinsman, out of affection; and an enemy, out of a desire for revenge. (Narada Smṛti 1.173)
Alternatively, even a single person who is agreed upon by two disputing parties may be questioned as a witness in the assembly, provided he is otherwise disqualified from being a witness.
But he who, because he is pierced by his own defects, appears as if unwell,
should move from one place to another and seek refuge with each one in turn.
He coughs uncontrollably and unexpectedly, sighs repeatedly, scratches the ground with his feet, and tosses his arms and garments about. (Nar_1.176)
The color of his face changes, and likewise his forehead perspires;
his lips become parched, and he gazes upward and sideways. (Nar 1.177)
He who speaks much without being asked, as if in haste and without foundation, should be known as a false witness; the king shall punish that sinner.
And he who, having caused others to hear [the testimony], then denies his witnesshood, must be punished even more severely; for he is worse than a false witness. (Narada 1.179)
Having summoned the witnesses, he should question them individually after restraining them with solemn oaths— those who are all of known conduct and who have knowledge of the matter.
One should cause a Brahmin to swear by truth, a Kṣatriya by his vehicle and weapons,
a Vaiśya by his cattle, grain, and gold, and a Śūdra by all the great sins.
Having greatly terrified the witnesses with ancient declarations of dharma, with praises of the greatness of truth, and with censures of falsehood; Nar_1.182.
Naked, shaven-headed, carrying a skull-bowl, tormented by hunger and thirst, and wretched, he who gives false testimony shall go to the house of his enemy as a beggar. (Narada 1.183)
He who gives false testimony shall be imprisoned in the city, hungry at the outer gate, and shall behold his enemies once again. (Nar_1.184)

The night that a woman is wedded, the night that one is defeated at dice, and the night that one’s limbs are tormented by a heavy burden—the speaker of falsehood shall dwell through them all. (Nar_1.185)
A witness who behaves with laxity like an ox's ear during the presentation of testimony binds a thousand nooses of Varuṇa upon himself. (Nar_1.186)
When a hundred years of that period have passed, one noose is released;
in this manner, he is liberated from that bondage after millions of years.
Listen, gentle one, to the number of kinsmen he slays by speaking falsely in testimony, in due order and according to their respective ranks. ||| Nar_1.188 |||
One kills five by lying about cattle, ten by lying about cows, a hundred by lying about horses, and a thousand by lying about men. (Nar_1.189)
One who speaks falsehood for the sake of gold destroys both those born and those unborn;
one destroys everything by speaking falsehood regarding land. Therefore, do not speak falsely regarding land. (Nar_1.190)
They say that truth alone is the singular, peerless purifier of the self; it is the staircase to heaven, like a boat for crossing from this shore to the other. (Narashanshiya 1.191)
A thousand horse-sacrifices and truth were once held upon a scale;
indeed, truth alone outweighed the thousand horse-sacrifices. (Nar_1.192)
A single well is better than a hundred pits; a sacrifice is better than a hundred wells;
a son is better than a hundred sacrifices; and truth is better than a hundred sons.
The earth supports all by means of truth; by truth the sun rises;
by truth the wind blows; and by truth the waters flow. (Nar_1.194)
Truth alone is the supreme gift; truth alone is the supreme austerity;
truth alone is the highest dharma for the worlds—thus have we heard. (Nar_1.195)
In brief, O gods, truth is the mark of humans, while falsehood is traditionally said to belong to them;
yet for one whose mind is established in truth, divinity exists even in this very world.
Speak the truth, having abandoned falsehood; by the truth you shall go to heaven.
Having spoken a most terrible lie, one will fall into hell.
And in the hells, those powerful and cruel servants of Yama will constantly cut out your tongue and sever it with swords.
Enraged, they will pierce with spears the one who cries out for refuge and has no protector;
lifting him up with his head downward, they will hurl him into pits of fire.
And having experienced those long-lasting sufferings of hell,
you will go here to the wombs of unworthy creatures such as vultures, crows, and the like.
Having understood these faults in falsehood and having understood the excellent qualities in truth, speak the truth and uplift yourself; do not cause yourself to fall.
Neither kinsmen, nor friends, nor even great riches are able to rescue one who is sinking into the fierce darkness. (Nar_1.202)
The ancestors, however, look up to you now that you have become their witness:
"Will he deliver us, or will he cause himself to fall? (Nar_1.203)
Truth is the self of man; everything is established upon truth.
In every way, you shall unite yourself with your own self through what is beneficial.
The interval between the night you were born and the night you will die would be spent in vain, if you were to act otherwise than according to the truth. (Nar_1.205)
There is no dharma higher than truth, and no sin greater than falsehood; especially in the matter of witness-hood, one should therefore speak only the truth. (Narada Smṛti 1.206)
That lowest of men who wields his own speech against the interests of others—what evil would he not do for his own sake, being fearless of hell? (Nar_1.207)
Meanings are indeed fixed in speech; they have speech as their root and have issued forth from speech.
For that man who would steal this speech is a thief of everything. (Nar_1.208)
But when witnesses disagree, the majority is the authority;
if they are equal in number, those who are pure should be accepted; if they are equal in purity, those with the better memory are to be relied upon.
But where, in a legal dispute, an equality of memory is observed among the witnesses,
the testimony is set aside again because of the subtle nature of the requirements for witness-status.

When the various matters have been set forth and the witness has arrived to testify, if he does not speak in accordance with the facts, that testimony shall not be considered properly delivered. (Narada 1.211)
In cases where there is disagreement regarding place, time, age, substance, quantity, appearance, or caste, that testimony is said to be invalid. (Narada 1.212)
Whatever matter the witnesses may state as deficient or excessive, that too is to be understood as unspoken; this is declared to be the rule for witnesses. (Narada 1.213)
Where, due to negligence, there is neither a document nor witnesses for a wealthy man, and the plaintiff denies the matter, there the threefold procedure has been declared. (Narada 1.214)
An accusation at the proper time, a fragment of reasoning, and likewise a third, an oath—by these means one should establish the case in due order. (Narada 1.215)
If one who is being repeatedly exhorted should reject those words,
then after three, four, or five times, one should bring that person to the truth.

But when there is an obstruction to the injunction, one should pursue it by means of fragments of reasoning through [considerations of] place, time, the relation of objects, magnitude, action, and so forth. (Nar_1.217)
Even when arguments are ineffective, one should distress him with oaths,
taking into account the nature of the matter, the time, and the strength of the case, by means of fire, water, meritorious deeds, and so forth.
He whom a blazing fire does not burn and whom the waters do not carry away crosses over the curse; in the opposite case, he shall be a sinner.
This same rule is seen to apply to women in cases of offenses against their character, as well as in theft and acts of violence, and in all instances of denial of one's own property. (Narada 1.220)
For even oaths are recorded as having been taken by the gods and the sages;
Vasiṣṭha, for instance, uttered a curse when he was suspicious of a Yātudhāna.
Then the Seven Sages, having assembled at Puṣkara for the sake of Indra,
uttered an oath with undistracted minds for the sake of mutual purification.
If one who has committed an improper act of violence seeks reconciliation,
or speaks for himself in the assembly, it is ordained that his punishment shall be half.
But if, out of wickedness, he conceals his sin, he shall be defeated; the members of the assembly are not satisfied with this, and a severe punishment is inflicted. (Nar_1.224)
2. *Nikṣepa*:
Where one deposits one's own property out of trust and without hesitation—that is called by the wise the legal head of dispute known as "deposit. (Nar_2.01)
When an object that is separated by other substances and is morally neutral (avyākṛta) is deposited in another's house, that is known as a sealed deposit (aupanidhika). (Narada 2.02)
Furthermore, that [loan] is said to be of two kinds: with witnesses and otherwise;
likewise, in the case of the opposite, there should be proof through restoration.
But he who, when requested by the depositor, does not return the deposit, shall be punished by the king and compelled to pay it; and if it has been lost, he shall be made to pay its equivalent.
And whoever should realize a profit from that [deposit] without the permission of the depositor,
he too shall be punished and must restore that [profit] along with interest.
If that which was lost along with the object of the borrower is destroyed by fate or by the king, it is lost for the owner, provided it was not caused by his own dishonesty. (Narada 2.06)
This same rule is seen to apply to articles borrowed or held in trust, as well as to craftsmen, deposits, pledges, and counter-pledges. (Narada 2.07)
This same duty applies to that man who adopts a minor son along with his property;
these six rules are equal. (Nar_2.08)
3. Partnership in Undertaking:
When merchants and others perform an enterprise collectively, that is known as the legal head of dispute called "partnership in undertaking. (Narada 3.01)
For those who, for the sake of the fruit, perform their actions in conjunction with skillful means, the [karmic] deposit serves as the support; by that, they may arise from their respective portions.
Whatever portion of anything is equal, superior, or inferior, its depletion, expenditure, and increase will likewise be of that same kind. (Nar_3.03)
Established in their own duty without deviation, they shall carry out the inspection of merchandise, the collection of dues, the recovery of expenditures, and the assessment of loads and quality.

He who, through negligence, causes loss, as well as he who performs what is forbidden, and he who acts without being instructed—all these must be made to pay by those who act in combination. (Narada 3.05)
When a calamity arising from gods, thieves, or the king has occurred, he who protects [a person] by his own power is declared to be entitled to a tenth share of the reward. (Narada 3.06)
If one person should meet with misfortune, his heir shall receive that [property];
or, in the absence of an heir, all those who are capable [of protecting it] shall do so.
Likewise, even upon the misfortune of the officiating priests, another may complete that rite;
he shall receive the portion of the sacrificial fee as it was assigned from that [total]. (Narada 3.08)
If a priest should abandon a patron who is blameless and has done him no wrong, or if a patron should abandon a blameless priest, both of them must be punished. (Narada 3.09)

The officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) is seen to be of three kinds: one appointed by ancestors, one chosen by oneself, and one who performs the priestly office out of his own accord and with affection. (Narada 3.10)
This rule applies when the officiating priests have been chosen according to tradition or by oneself;
however, if the priests are engaged at one's own discretion, there is no sin in dismissing them.
When a merchant arrives at a customs station, he should pay the toll as it is prescribed;
he must not evade it, for this is ordained as a tribute to the kings. (Nar_3.12)
One who evades the customs office, one who buys or sells outside the prescribed time,
or one who declares a false quantity, shall be made to pay an eightfold fine as a penalty.
If some merchant, while traveling from his country, should die as an arrival [in another land], the king shall protect his merchandise until his heirs appear. (Narada 3.14)
If there is no heir, one should entrust that property to kinsmen or relatives;
in their absence, one should keep it well-guarded for ten years.
After ten years have passed, that which has no owner and no heir, the king may take for himself; in this way, the law is not violated. (Nar_3.16)
4.1 Having given property, he who then desires to take it back because it was not properly given—
that is known in legal treatises as the title of dispute called *dattāpradānika* (non-delivery of what has been given).

That which is not to be given, that which is to be given, that which has been given, and that which has not been given—these fourfold paths of giving are to be understood in legal proceedings. (Nar_4.02)
For in that regard, eight things are traditionally held to be non-givable, and the givable is said to be of one kind;
one should know that what is given is of seven kinds, while the ungiven consists of sixteen types.
That which has been deposited with another, that which has been borrowed, a pledge, property held in common, a trust, one's wife and children, and one's entire estate when there is offspring; 4.04.

For even when a living being is beset by dire calamities, the teachers declare that certain things must not be given away—specifically, that which has already been promised to another. (Narashanshiya 4.05)
Whatever wealth remains after supporting one's family should be given away;
if one gives something else after withholding that [remainder], one incurs fault. (Nar_4.06)

Those who know the rules of giving recognize as a gift what is given for the price of merchandise, as wages, out of satisfaction, out of affection, as a return favor, or for the sake of a bride-price or to show favor. (Nar_4.07)
But what is taken without it being given may be so through the force of fear, anger, grief, or illness;
likewise, it may be through bribery, jesting, exchange, or by means of fraud. (Nar_4.08)

That which is performed by one who is a child, deluded, lacking independence, afflicted, intoxicated, or insane; and that which is done with the desire for gain, thinking, "This person is my agent" and "this is my deed. (Naraka 4.09)

If one calls an unworthy recipient worthy, or performs an act associated with unrighteousness, whatever is given therein through ignorance is considered, according to the legal tradition, as not given at all. (Narada 4.10)

He who, out of greed, takes what is not given, and he who bestows what ought not to be given—both the thief of the ungiven and the giver of that which should not be given are to be punished. (Narada 4.11)
5. Breach of Service:
But when one who has undertaken service does not perform it, this legal dispute regarding the breach of service after having undertaken it is thus described. (Narada 5.01)
In the treatise, the wise have observed five kinds of attendants;
four kinds of laborers, and fifteen kinds of slaves among them. (Nar_5.02)

The pupil, the resident student, and the hired servant—these three, along with the fourth, the laborer for extra work, are called "workmen" (karmakara); whereas slaves (dāsa) are those born in the house and so forth. (Narada 5.03)
The wise say that their lack of independence is their common characteristic;
however, the distinctions among them, as well as their specific modes of livelihood, are said to be determined by birth and action.
Action, too, should be known to be of two kinds: indeed, the unwholesome and the wholesome.
The unwholesome is said to be the work of a slave, while the wholesome is remembered as the work of those who act with virtue.

The cleaning of house doors, impure places, streets, and refuse heaps; the touching of private parts, the handling of food remnants, and the taking up and discarding of feces and urine. // Nar_5.06 //
Furthermore, the worship of one's master with one's own limbs according to his desire is to be known as inauspicious action; other than that, everything else is auspicious.
Until he has acquired knowledge, the disciple should serve his guru with self-restraint;
he should behave toward the wife and the son of the guru in exactly the same manner. (Narada Smṛti 5.08)
A student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) should subsist on alms, sleep on the ground, remain unadorned,
go to bed last of all, and rise before everyone else while living in the house of his teacher.
One should not set out on a journey or remain anywhere near one's teacher without being instructed;
once instructed, if one is capable, one should perform the task without hesitation.
One should study at the proper time as long as the teacher is not troubled in mind;
seated below the teacher on a grass mat or a wooden plank, one should remain composed.
If one who is to be instructed by a teacher does not comply,
he should be punished without causing physical injury, using either a rope or a split bamboo cane.
One should not strike him excessively, nor on the head or the chest;
having instructed him and gained his confidence, he may then be disciplined by the king, otherwise like a teacher.
And having returned home after presenting the teacher’s fee to the guru, he should go to his own house; this is declared to be the conduct of a student.
Desiring to acquire his own craft with the permission of his kinsmen, he should dwell in the presence of a teacher for a well-determined period of time. (Nar_5.15)
The teacher should instruct him, providing him with food from his own home;
he should not make him perform any other labor, and should treat him like a son. (Nar_5.16)
He who abandons a teacher who is instructing him and is free from malice shall be compelled to dwell [with him] by force, and he deserves both corporal punishment and imprisonment. (Nar_5.17)
Even if he has been trained, the pupil shall receive the agreed-upon fee once the time is completed;
furthermore, whatever work he performs therein, the fruit thereof belongs solely to the teacher. (Nar_5.18)
Once he has mastered the craft, the pupil, having circumambulated the teacher at the proper time and honored him according to his ability, should take his leave. (Nar_5.19)
A hired servant should be known to be of three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior.
Their wages, based on their work, should correspond to their ability and devotion. (Narada 5.20)
Among these, the warrior is the highest, the cultivator is middling, and the porter is the lowest; thus is the hired laborer of three kinds. (Narada 5.21)
He who is authorized over matters concerning the household is to be known as an *adhikarmakara*; he is also remembered as a *kauṭumbika*. (Nar_5.22)
These four are declared to be performers of auspicious deeds;
however, the remaining fifteen types of servants partake in inferior occupations.
One born in the house, one purchased, one obtained, one received as an heir, one supported during a time of distress, and likewise one who was conceived by the master— Nar_5.24.
"Rescued from great bondage, won back from battle as a prize, and having approached you saying 'I am yours,' I have been made to dwell in the life of a wandering mendicant. (Nar_5.25)
One who becomes a slave for food, one supported by a female slave, and one who sells himself—these are declared in the treatise to be the fifteen kinds of slaves. (Narada 5.26)
In that regard, the first four classes are not released from servitude except through the favor of their master; for them, servitude is hereditary. (Nar_5.27)
And whoever should liberate their master from a life-threatening danger shall be released from servitude and receive a share equal to that of a son. (Nar_5.28)
One who has maintained a slave during a time of famine is released from servitude by giving a pair of cattle;
however, that which was consumed during a famine cannot be purified by such an act.
Even if he has been pledged after receiving a price, if the owner should redeem him, then one should restore him; he is next in rank to one who was sold. (Narada 5.30)
Having paid back the debt along with interest, the debtor is released from slavery;
even one who was made a slave by agreement is released once the stipulated time has passed. (Nar_5.31)
Having approached you saying "I am yours," and having been won at the stake when the battle was joined,
he is released by the giving of a counter-head through an equal act.
But a man who has fallen from the religious life shall become the slave of the king alone;
for him there is no release from that state, nor any purification whatsoever.
By neglecting his devotee, a master is instantly released from the state of being a slave to that devotee;
and by the restraint of the mare, the one who maintains the mare is released from his obligation.
That lowest of men who, being independent, sells himself—he is the most wretched of them all and is never released from servitude. (Nar_5.35)
Those who have been stolen by thieves, sold, or forcibly enslaved, must be liberated by the king; servitude is not permitted for them. (Nar_5.36)
Servitude is not ordained through the inverse order of the castes;
except for one who has abandoned their own duty, servitude is considered to be like [the taking of] a wife.
He who, being himself not independent, offers himself up saying "I am yours," shall not obtain that desired object; the former master shall regain him.
Only three are declared to be without property: the wife, the slave, and likewise the son;
whatever they acquire belongs to him to whom they themselves belong. (Narada 5.39)
If one, with a joyful mind, should wish to make his own slave a non-slave, he should take a water-pot from that person's shoulder and break it along with its water. (Nar_5.40)
One should sprinkle him on the head with unbroken grains and flowers; then, having said "He is no longer a slave," one should release him facing eastward three times. (Nar_5.41)
From that time forward, he should be addressed as one protected by the favor of his master;
he becomes one whose food may be eaten, one who may accept gifts, and one who is held in high esteem.
6. Non-payment of Wages: The prescribed procedure for the giving and receiving of wages for those who have been employed has been stated;
the non-payment of such wages is recorded as that title of dispute. (Narada 6.1)
The employer of laborers shall pay their wages according to the sequence agreed upon—whether at the beginning, the middle, or the end of the work—as has been determined. (Narada 6.2)
But when the wages are not fixed, the merchant, the cowherd, and the cultivator shall each receive a tenth part of the profit,
the cattle, the seed, and the crop, respectively.
Whatever implements for work have been brought for their task, he should employ them with a sense of trustworthiness;
he should not act with deceit.

One who, having promised to perform work, does not do it; or one who, having received wages, performs work by force; or one who, having received wages, does not perform the work—he shall pay double the wages. 6.5.
If he should abandon his work before the time is completed, he deserves the loss of his wages;
however, if he departs due to a fault of the master, he shall receive payment for what he has already done.
Having agreed upon a wage consisting of a sixth part of the produce, if he abandons a laborer on the road while using his vehicle,
or if he makes him work without paying, he must pay the wage along with interest.
If one hires carriers for goods by means of vehicles or draft animals, they must be made to pay a fourth part of the wages; however, if one abandons them midway, they shall pay half.
Likewise, a carrier who fails to bring [the goods] shall suffer a loss of wages;
however, one who creates an obstacle to the departure shall be made to pay double the wages.
If the goods should meet with misfortune due to the fault of the carrier,
he shall be made to pay for whatever has been lost, except in cases caused by fate or the king.
From a hundred cows, a heifer shall be the cowherd's fee; from two hundred, the milk for one day;
and every year, on the eighth day, he shall receive the entire yield of milk.
"O cowherd, you must bring back the cows every day at the end of the night;
having grazed and drunk, the cowherd shall bring them back in the evening. (Nar_6.12)
If a calamity should befall the cattle, the cowherd should strive to remedy it to the best of his ability;
if he is unable, he should quickly return and report it to his master. (Narada 6.13)
If he does not exert himself to recover it, nor cries out for help, nor informs his owner,
the cowherd must pay the value of that [lost] animal and also a fine to the king.
