One should cause a cow that is lost, destroyed, infested with worms, struck by a dog, dead in a precarious place,
or deficient in human effort to be returned to the owner alone.
If goats and sheep are thus obstructed by wolves and the herdsman does not come to their aid,
whatever wolf may kill by force, the guilt for that shall fall upon the herdsman.
And while they were wandering together in the forest, unobstructed, if a wolf should spring upon and kill one of them, the herdsman would not be at fault in that matter. (Nar_6.17)
If cattle have been stolen by thieves after being publicly proclaimed, the herdsman is not liable to pay,
provided he reports it to his own master at the proper place and time.
By this, the dispute regarding all guardians has been explained;
and in the case of those who have died, purification shall occur upon the sight of their marks and other signs.
If a courtesan, having accepted a fee, does not wish to comply, she shall pay double that amount;
likewise, a man who has enjoyed a woman but fails to pay the fee shall suffer the same penalty.
He who approaches a woman in a non-vaginal passage, or causes her to dwell with many men,
shall be made to pay eightfold the nuptial fee and an equal amount as a fine.

If one who has built a house on another's threshing floor should dwell there after having offered a hymn of praise, he must take away that house—its grass, wood, bricks, and so forth—and depart. (Nar_6.22)
One should bring forward the vessels that carry the soma-juice when they are full at the appointed time;
otherwise, what is broken or lost shall be the responsibility of the receiver, except in the case of an accident.
7. Sale by One Who Is Not the Owner:
When property belonging to another—whether deposited, lost, found, or stolen—is sold in the absence of the owner, it should be known as "sale by one who is not the owner. (Narada 7.1)
Having recovered property sold by one who is not its owner, the true owner shall take possession of it;
the buyer is cleared of guilt if the purchase was made openly, but the act is theft if the purchase was made in secret.

One who buys a slave from one who is not the master, from a dishonest person, or in secret; or who buys at an inadequate price or at an improper time, shall incur the guilt of that [fraudulent transaction]. (Narada 7.3)
The purchaser should not conceal the source of his acquisition; his purity is established by that provenance.
In the opposite case, he incurs the same fault and deserves the punishment for theft.
In the case of a sale without ownership, the seller shall restore the object to the owner and pay the price paid by the buyer;
likewise, he shall pay a fine to the king—this is the rule regarding sale without ownership.
If one finds a treasure deposited by another, he should present it to the king;
for all treasure belongs to the king, with the exception of a Brāhmaṇa. (Narada 7.6)
A Brahmin, having found a treasure-trove, should also quickly report it to the king;
he may enjoy what is given by him, for by failing to report it, he would be a thief. (Narada 7.7)
If he recovers even his own lost property and reports it to the king, he shall be considered pure in that matter; otherwise, he would be deemed impure. (Narada 7.8)
8. Rescission of Purchase: When, after having sold a commodity for its price, it is not delivered to the buyer, that is called the legal title of "Non-delivery after Sale. (Narada 8.1)
In this world, there are two kinds of substances: the mobile and the immobile; all of these are called "merchandise" (paṇya) in the context of the laws of buying and selling. (Nar_8.2)
The wise have declared that his method for giving and receiving is sixfold:
by counting, by weighing, by measuring, and by action, by form, and by beauty.
If one who has sold a commodity does not deliver it to the buyer for its price,
he shall be made to pay the loss of value for an immovable thing, and the fruit of its use for a movable thing.
If the profit margin should be lost, one should recover the merchandise together with the interest;
this is the rule for stationary traders, while those who travel in various directions receive a share according to their respective regions.
If the merchandise should be damaged, burnt, or stolen, that loss falls upon the seller alone for having sold it without delivering it. (Narada 8.6)
But he who, having shown an item as faultless, delivers one that is defective,
shall be made to pay double its value and undergo a fine of the same amount.
Likewise, he who sells [an item] into the hand of one person and then delivers it to another shall be made to pay double that amount and be punished to the same extent.
If a buyer does not accept a commodity being offered for sale, or if a seller sells it elsewhere after having already agreed to sell it, neither shall be held at fault. (Narada 8.9)
This rule has been proclaimed regarding merchandise for which the price has been paid;
if it is not delivered, except by mutual agreement, there is no transgression on the part of the seller. (Narada 8.10)
For the sake of profit, merchants engage in the buying and selling of all commodities; yet that profit, depending on the market price, may or may not become great. (Nar_8.11)
Therefore, in that place and at that time, a merchant should investigate the market price;
he should not proceed by crooked means, for such is the superior path of trade.
9.1. Non-delivery after sale:
When a buyer, having purchased a commodity for a price, does not regard it as being of value, this is called the legal head of dispute known as "repentance after purchase."
If a buyer, having purchased a commodity for a price, considers it a bad purchase,
it must be returned to the seller on that very same day, provided it is still unspoiled.
If the purchaser delivers it on the second day, he shall pay a thirtieth part of the price as a fine;
on the third day, that fine is doubled; beyond that, the property belongs to the purchaser alone.
A buyer should personally examine a commodity beforehand for its merits and defects;
once it has been examined and purchased with approval, it cannot be returned to the seller.
One should examine what is to be milked after three days, but what is to be carried on a beast of burden after five;
however, for pearls, diamonds, and corals, the examination period shall be seven days.
For bipeds, the period shall be half a month for males and double that for females;
for all seeds, it is ten days; and for metals and clothes, it is one day.
Furthermore, a garment that has been worn, which is faded, soiled, and even defective, once sold, shall not belong to the seller again. (Nar_9.7)

The value of a garment that has been washed once is reduced by one-eighth; after a second washing, it is reduced by one-half; after a third, by one-third; and after a fourth, by one-half [of its original value]. (Narada 9.8)
But beyond the point when half has decayed, there is a gradual reduction by one-quarter at each stage until it reaches the state of being worn out;
for that which is worn out, there is no fixed rule regarding its further decay.
Even for all metals, when they are being refined through the process of heating by fire, their depletion is observed to result from contact with that fire. (Nar_9.10)
There is no loss in the case of gold; for silver, there is a loss of two palas per hundred;
it should be known that for tin and lead, the loss is eight palas per hundred. (Nar_9.11)
One should know that five palas [of ash] result from copper, as well as from whatever alloys are made thereof;
because there are many such metals, there is no fixed rule regarding the reduction of iron. (Nar_9.12)
Regarding the processing of woven cloth, the decrease and increase have been illustrated:
for threads made of cotton or wool, there is an increase of ten palas for every hundred.
For those of medium thickness like thick threads, five hundred [turns] are prescribed;
for very fine threads, three palas are declared to be the limit at the end of their consumption.
For that which is pierced by a needle, the loss is one-thirtieth of what was produced by the work;
however, for silks and bark garments, there is neither increase nor decrease.
A merchant skilled in trade should not harbor regret after purchasing;
rather, he should understand the fluctuations in value and the supply of his wares. (Nar_9.16)
The established rule of heretics, guilds, and the like is called a *samaya*. The failure to fulfill such a rule is recorded as a ground for dispute (*vivādapada*). (Narada 10.1)
The king shall likewise protect the established conventions among heretics, guilds, corporations, associations, bands, and assemblies, as well as within forts and the countryside. (Narada Smṛti 10.2)
Whatever the duty, whatever the action, whatever the manner of attendance, and whatever the means of livelihood for these [ascetics], one should approve of that accordingly. (Nar_10.3)
Whatever is contrary to the king's wishes, whatever is naturally despised by his subjects, and whatever is detrimental to his interests— he should turn those things away from them.
The king should not tolerate their forming secret conspiracies, their bearing of weapons, or their mutual injury toward one another. (Nar_10.5)
Those who would divide the separate groups must be especially disciplined;
for if they are neglected, they will bring about terrible danger, like a disease. (Nar_10.6)
Whatever instrument of action is defective and not ordained by the sacred tradition,
the king who desires his own welfare should cause it to be stopped, even if it has already been set in motion.

Where there are determinations regarding embankments, field boundaries, and the distinction between cultivated and uncultivated land, as well as matters concerning the management of fields—that is a dispute arising from fields. (Narada 11.1)
In disputes concerning the boundaries of fields, the decision is reached based on the testimony of the neighbors,
the heads of cities, villages, and guilds, and those men who are the most venerable.
And those who live outside the village boundaries by means of agriculture, as well as cowherds, fowlers, hunters, and others who dwell in the forest; 11.3.
They should mark out the boundary, characterized by husks, charcoal, potsherds, water-jars, shrines, and trees. (Nar_11.4)
And by means of well-known anthills, level ground, depressions, and elevations, as well as old irrigation channels, groves, paths, and embankments; (Nar_11.5)

On lands where the marks [of ownership] have been lost because they were swept away by river waters, [ownership is determined] by inferring those regions and by means of measurements and the observation of possession. (Narada 11.6)
But if the neighbors should speak falsely in determining that matter,
they shall all be punished individually by the king with the middle amercement.
But others, such as the head of a guild and so forth, shall each be made to pay a fine;
if they persist in falsehood, they are to be punished with the first amercement. (Narada 11.8)
A single man, even if he be trustworthy, shall not determine a boundary by himself; because of the gravity of this matter, this procedure is established upon many. (Narada 11.9)
If there is only one person [to establish] the boundary, he should do so while fasting and composed in mind, wearing red garlands and garments, having placed the earth upon his head. (Nar_11.10)
And when there are no knowers of the boundary nor any characteristic mark, then the king himself shall determine the boundary between the two [villages] as he deems fit. (Nar_11.11)

By this very same rule, the procedure for resolving disputes regarding houses, gardens, water reservoirs, temples, and so forth, as well as those between different villages, has been declared. (Narada 11.12)
One should not obstruct crossroads, temples, or main roads with refuse heaps, pits, ditches, drains, and the like. (Narada Smṛti 11.13)
A boundary embankment in the middle of another's field is not prohibited, provided it yields great benefit with little harm; for when there is loss, an increase is desired. 11.14.
A dam is to be known as being of two kinds: that which is to be dug out (kheya) and likewise that which is to be bound (bandhya).
That which is to be dug out is for the purpose of directing the flow of water; that which is to be bound is for the purpose of stopping it. (Nar_11.15)
Without water, the crop would perish; yet by excessive water it likewise perishes.
That very same fault which exists in the absence of water is recorded as existing in the case of excessive water.
But whoever should attempt to construct a dam that was previously begun and then abandoned, without having consulted his master, shall not partake in its fruit. (Narada 11.17)
But when the master has died, or even when a descendant of his lineage is no longer among men,
one should then consult the king and carry out that work of constructing the embankment.
Otherwise, one would be subject to affliction, as seen in the case of the hunter;
for him who pierces again what has already been pierced, his arrows are wasted. (Nar 11.19)
If someone should cultivate a field that has been abandoned by its owner due to incapacity, death, or disappearance, he may enjoy the fruit thereof without being hindered. (Narada 11.20)
If the owner of a field returns while it is being ploughed, he shall recover his own field by paying for all the cultivation of the fallow land. (Narada 11.21)
Then, through a reduction of one-eighth each year until seven years have passed, he shall obtain possession of that field once the eighth year has arrived. (Nar_11.22)
In one year, a field becomes half-waste; in three years, it becomes completely waste; but a field neglected for five years becomes like a wilderness. (Narada 11.23)

If there be a field or a house that has passed down through three generations, or one obtained through the favor of a king—except in these cases—one should not transfer the enjoyment of such property to another. (Narada 11.24)
But where crops are destroyed by cattle and other animals after they have broken through the enclosure,
the keeper shall be punished, provided he did not prevent it to the best of his ability.
But when there is destruction of standing crops along with their roots, the owner of those crops shall receive an equal amount as compensation;
the herdsman shall be released from blame by killing [the offending animal], but he shall inflict the fine upon the owner. (Narada 11.26)
A cow that has recently calved, as well as bulls, goats, sheep, and elephants, must be kept away [from the field] with great effort for ten days; their owner shall not be subject to punishment.
One should cause a fine of one *māṣa* to be paid for a cow, two *māṣas* for a buffalo, and a fine of half a *māṣa* for a goat or sheep, provided they are with their young. (Narada 11.28)
Elephants and horses are not to be punished, for they are considered protectors of the subjects;
likewise, a cow that is pregnant, one that has recently calved, and one that is in heat are exempt from punishment.
For those who sit twice [in the same manner], the punishment is declared to be double; for those who live there [as spies], it is fourfold.
Likewise, the punishment for a thief is ordained for those who act as direct spies.
If cows that have strayed due to the fault of the herdsman take refuge in a field, the owner of the field shall not be punished; rather, the herdsman deserves that punishment. (Narada 11.31)
Whether seized by a king's grasping, or struck by a thunderbolt, or bitten by a serpent, or even fallen from the peak of a mountain; (Nar_11.32)
Even if [the animal] is killed by lions or tigers, or struck down by diseases, there is no fault on the part of the keeper, nor is there any fault for the owners. (Narada 11.33)
If a man seeks to recover grain that has been eaten by cows, the neighbor must pay the fine for the damage, and the grain that was sown there must be given to the owner of the cows;
however, fodder for the cows must be given to the farmer. (Nar_11.34)
And if a field located on the outskirts of a village, at the edge of a pasture, or by a great road is uncovered, there is no fault on the part of the guardian if it is destroyed. (Narada 11.35)
On the path, a fence should be constructed such that a camel cannot look over it, nor can a beast, a horse, or even a boar leap over or break through it. (Nar_11.36)
A house and a field should be known as the basis for the residence of householders;
therefore, the king should not confiscate them, for they are the very root of the householders' livelihood. (Nar_11.37)
In a flourishing realm, the king’s righteousness and treasury increase; when it declines, they too diminish. Therefore, he should rely upon the causes of prosperity. (Nar 11.38)
That title of dispute in which the rites of marriage and so forth for women and men are proclaimed is called *strīpuṃsayoga*. (Narada 12.1)
From the union of a woman and a man, the formal choosing (*varaṇa*) is prescribed first;
after the choosing comes the grasping of the hand (*pāṇigrahaṇa*), and then the twofold sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*). (Narada 12.2)
For those two, marriage is said to be indefinite because of the possibility of perceiving faults;
however, the status of being a wife is made definite by the taking of the hand and the recitation of the mantras. (Nar_12.3)
Among the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, for the purpose of taking a wife, a woman of one's own caste is superior; and for a woman, a husband of her own caste is likewise superior.
For a Brāhmaṇa, there are three other wives in the direct order [of castes];
likewise, for a Śūdra, there are three other husbands in the inverse order. (Nar_12.5)
Two wives are prescribed for a Kṣatriya, and one for a Vaiśya.
It should be known that a Vaiśya may have two husbands, while a Kṣatriya has only one.
Up to the seventh or the fifth degree from the paternal and maternal relatives, those of the same *gotra* as well as those with the same *pravara* are ineligible for marriage. (Narada 12.7)
A man must be examined for his virility by the very characteristics of his own limbs;
if he is a male without deficiency, he is worthy to receive a maiden.
His collarbones, knees, and bones were well-knit; his shoulders and neck were firm;
his temples were broad, his thighs were slender, and his skin was thin; his gait and voice were unhindered.
If his semen floats on water and his urine is pleasant-smelling and frothy, he shall be a man; by the opposite characteristics, however, he is a eunuch. (Nar_12.10)
In the treatise, that [disease] is seen by the wise to be of fourteen kinds;
the method for treating those that are curable and those that are incurable has been stated in due order. (Nar_12.11)
One who is impotent by nature, one who is a eunuch, and likewise one who is impotent for a period;
as well as one rendered so by a teacher’s curse, by disease, or by the wrath of the gods. (Nar_12.12)

The envious eunuch, the one who must be served, the one with wind-semen, the one whose mouth is his vulva, the one who is rejected, the one with sterile seed, the bashful, and likewise the one whose master is another. (Nar_12.13)
Among these, the first two are incurable; one should observe the treatment known as *pakṣa* for a month.
For this triad [of diseases], the duration is traditionally recorded as one year in successive order.
The other four qualities that have been proclaimed—envy, malice, and so forth—must be abandoned by a woman whose womb has been violated, just as one would treat a fallen man. (Nar_12.15)
If her husband is unable to perform his duties and has sown infertile seeds,
another man is permitted for the woman after she has waited for one year.

Even the banner of a modest man may break through union with an audacious woman; therefore, one should employ other women, such as young girls and the like, against him when his vigor has diminished. (Nar_12.17)
If a man who belongs to another should act like a non-human toward his own wife, she may obtain another husband; this is the ordinance of Prajāpati.
Women were created for the sake of offspring; a woman is the field for the seed-bearer, and progeny belongs to the one who provides the seed.
The field should be given to the one possessing the seed; he who has no seed does not deserve the field.
The father himself should give away the maiden, or the brother with the father’s consent;
likewise the maternal grandfather, the maternal uncle, the paternal kinsmen, and other relatives. (Narada 12.20)
But in the absence of a mother, if she [the paternal grandmother] is present in her natural state,
then when she is not in that natural state, members of their own caste shall give the girl in marriage.
But when there is no one at all [suitable], the maiden may approach the king; with his permission, having fixed upon a bridegroom, she may choose him herself. (Nar_12.22)
He should practice dharma together with a wife who is of the same caste and similar in lineage, appearance, age, and learning; and from her, he should procreate sons.
If a man who has accepted a maiden should depart for another country,
and after three menstrual seasons have passed, she may choose another groom.
A maiden may disregard her desire to dance; she should inform her kinsmen.
If they do not give her to a husband, they shall be equal to killers of embryos.
As many seasons as have passed for her without a husband, so many instances of foeticide shall belong to him who does not give her away. (Nar_12.26)
Therefore, before the onset of menstruation, the father should give his daughter away once;
otherwise, he incurs a great sin—such is the rule for the virtuous.
A share of inheritance falls but once; a daughter is given away but once;
one says "I give" but once—these three things happen only once each.
The prescribed rule is recorded for these five forms of marriage beginning with the Brāhma;
in the three beginning with the Āsura, the giving [of the bride] depends upon [the groom's] qualities.

If a bridegroom who is superior arrives after the bride-price has already been received for a maiden, one may speak words concerning dharma, artha, and kāma; in that case, it would not be a falsehood.
One should not defile an unblemished maiden, nor should one defile an unblemished groom;
however, if a fault exists, there is no sin in those two abandoning each other.
If a man, having given his daughter according to the law, does not hand her over to the groom when she is faultless, he shall be punished by the king like a thief. (Narada 12.32)
But for him who gives away a daughter who has defects without disclosing them,
the king shall inflict the punishment prescribed for the first degree of violence.
But that man who, out of malice, declares a maiden to be "not a virgin" without demonstrating any fault in her, shall incur a fine of one hundred [paṇas]. (Narada Smṛti 12.34)
But a suitor who, having accepted an unblemished maiden, should abandon her,
must be disciplined even against his will and shall have to marry that very same girl again.

Afflicted by long-standing or loathsome diseases, physically deformed, having had sexual intercourse, impudent, and whose heart is set on another—these are proclaimed as the defects of a maiden. (Nar_12.36)
One who is insane, fallen from caste, impotent, unfortunate, or abandoned by kinsmen, as well as the two previously mentioned defects of a maiden—this is the group of defects in a groom. (Nar_12.37)
Eight forms of marriage have been proclaimed for the sacramental rites of the social classes;
of these, the Brāhma and likewise the Prājāpatya are the first.
The Ārṣa, the Daiva, the Gāndharva, and likewise the Āsura;
the Rākṣasa follows immediately after that, and the Paiśāca is recorded as the eighth.

Having honored the girl and invited her, one should give her away adorned with ornaments in the Brāhma rite; having said, "May you both perform your duties together," it is ordained as the Prājāpatya rite. (Nar_12.40)
Having given a pair of a cow and a bull, the marriage is called Ārṣa;
that which takes place within the sacrificial altar for the officiating priest performing the rite is Daiva. (Nar_12.41)
They say that when a man desires a woman who desires him, that is the fifth marriage, known as Gāndharva;
the Āsura form of marriage is to be understood as one involving the transaction of a bride-price.
Marriage by abduction is called the Rākṣasa form;
likewise, the eighth and lowest is the Paiśāca, resulting from approaching a woman while she is asleep or intoxicated.
Of these, the four beginning with the Brāhma are declared to be lawful;
the Gāndharva is common to all, while the three beyond it are unlawful.
Other women who have had previous husbands are said to be sevenfold in sequence;
among them, the *punarbhū* is of three kinds, while the *svairiṇī* is of four kinds. (Nar_12.45)

A maiden who, though her virginity remains intact, has been defiled by the taking of the hand in marriage, is called the first kind of *punarbhū* (a remarried woman); she is eligible for the marriage rite once again.
She who, having abandoned her husband from childhood, resorts to another man and then returns again to her husband's house, is proclaimed as the second [type]. (Nar_12.47)
When no brothers-in-law are present, the woman who is given by her kinsmen to a man of the same caste who is not a sapinda is proclaimed as the third [form of marriage].
Whether she has borne children or not, if a woman, while her husband is still living,
out of desire resorts to another man, she is the first type of unchaste woman (svairiṇī).

She who, upon the death of her husband, rejects even the brothers-in-law who have approached her and, out of desire, approaches another man, is proclaimed as the second [type of remarried woman]. (Nar_12.50)
She who has come from another land, purchased with wealth, and is afflicted by hunger and thirst, approaching you saying "I am yours"—she is proclaimed as the third type. (Nar_12.51)
A woman who, disregarding local customs, is given by her elders to one man but then acts with violence toward another,
is indeed remembered as a wanton woman (svairiṇī).
This rule has been proclaimed for women who have remarried and for wanton women;
among them, each preceding one is inferior, while each succeeding one is superior.
Regarding the procreation of offspring, the fruit belongs to him from whom she was taken for a price;
however, in the case of one who has approached her without a price, the fruit belongs to the owner of the field alone.
If seed is sown in a field without the knowledge of the owner of the field, there is no share for the owner of the seed; that [crop] belongs to the owner of the field alone. (Nar_12.55)

If a seed carried by the force of a flood sprouts in someone's field, that person who possesses the field is the one who enjoys the fruit; the owner of the seed shall not share in the fruit. (Nar_12.56)
If a great bull, while roaming among the cows in the pen, should sire calves, those cows belong to him;
for that bull, his virility has been in vain.
When seed, with the consent of the owner of the field, is sown in someone's field, that offspring is considered to belong to both the owner of the seed and the owner of the field. (Narada 12.58)
There would be no crop without a field, nor would it exist without a seed;
therefore, according to the law, offspring is held to belong to both the father and the mother.

Experts recognize adultery as occurring when a man who is under the protection of another is seen in union with a woman in another's house; it is not so recognized when she has come to his own house of her own accord.

There is no offense of violence in approaching the wife of one who is corrupt, one who has abandoned his wife, one who is impotent, or one who is submissive, provided she approaches him of her own accord.

Standing together with another man's wife at an improper time or in an improper place, conversing with her, or sharing amorous dalliance—these three constitute the stages of adultery (*saṃgrahaṇa*). (Narada 12.62)
When a woman and a man meet at the confluence of rivers, at sacred fords, in groves, or in forests, their union shall be considered adultery (*saṃgrahaṇa*).

By means of dispatching female messengers, by sending letters, and through other such transgressions as well, all such acts are recorded in the legal tradition as *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual intercourse with another's wife).
If one should touch a woman in an improper place, or likewise, if being touched he should reciprocate that touch with her consent, that shall constitute *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual intercourse).
Whether by means of foods, or edibles, or garments, or likewise garlands,
or by being sent perfumes— all such [acts] are recorded as seduction.
Whether out of pride, delusion, or self-praise, if one should say of her own accord,
"She was previously enjoyed by me," all such cases are recorded in the law as *saṃgrahaṇa* (adultery).
If one should seize another by the hand, or by the braid of hair, or even by the hem of the garment, or say "Stay! Stay!", all this is recorded as *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual misconduct).

When men violate their own caste, the punishment prescribed is the highest fine; in the reverse case, it is a middle fine; but when the violation is against a lower caste, it is the death penalty. (Narada 12.69)
If the maiden is unwilling, there shall be the cutting off of two fingers;
however, in the case of a woman of the highest caste, there shall indeed be execution as well as the confiscation of all her property.
But when a maiden is willing and he is of the same caste, there is no transgression; however, having adorned her and honored her, he alone shall marry her. (Nar_12.71)

A mother, a maternal aunt, a mother-in-law, a maternal uncle’s wife, a paternal aunt, the wife of a paternal uncle, a friend’s wife, a female disciple, a sister, her friend, and a daughter-in-law; Nar_12.72 //

A daughter, the wife of a teacher, one of the same lineage, one who has sought refuge, a queen, one who has gone forth into the religious life, a nurse, a virtuous woman, and she who is of the highest caste. || 12.73 ||
Having approached any one of these women, he is called a violator of the Guru's bed;
the punishment prescribed for him is the excision of the penis, and no other is ordained in that case. (Nar_12.74)
One who transgresses against an animal is to be disciplined with one hundred lashes;
for cows, the punishment is the middle amercement, and the same applies to those of the lowest castes.
The king, urged by the law, inflicts punishment upon one who approaches a woman who should not be approached;
in this matter, however, purification through the prescribed rite of atonement is the means of cleansing. (Nar_12.76)

A woman who is self-willed, a non-Brāhmaṇa woman, a courtesan, a female slave, and one who has left her husband— all these women may be approached in the direct order of castes (ānulomya), but never in the inverse order (pratiloma).
However, with these very female slaves, there would be the same fault as with the wives of others;
for even if they are approachable, one should not have intercourse with them if they belong to another.
If the husband of a woman who has not yet borne a child should die, she,
being authorized by her elders, may approach her brother-in-law out of a desire for a son.
He should proceed in that very manner until the birth of a son;
once a son is born, he may desist, for otherwise there would be a transgression.
Having anointed his limbs with clarified butter or unrefined oil, avoiding the contact of mouth with mouth and limb with limb, he should proceed. (Nar_12.81)

One should not approach a woman who has already borne a son, one who is barren, one who is menstruating, one who is unwilling, one who is pregnant, one who is censurable, or one who has not been authorized by her kinsmen. (Narada 12.82)

But if a woman, not authorized by her husband, should bear a son to her brother-in-law, those who speak according to the Dharma say that he is born of an adulterer and is not entitled to the inheritance. (Nar_12.83)
Likewise, if a younger brother approaches his elder brother's wife,
or an elder brother approaches his younger brother's wife, when neither has been so authorized, both of them are violators of the Guru’s bed.

When the family line remains only with that [last member], one who has been appointed by his elders for the sake of progeny—and not out of lust—may approach the wife of his younger brother. (Nar_12.85)
But if no guru is present, the king should be informed of the destruction of the family;
then, having been instructed by him, he should depart together with his wife.

Having bathed according to the very procedure previously described during the *puṃsavana* rite, the pure man—whether once or until conception has occurred—regards her as his own daughter-in-law once the embryo is formed. (Nar_12.87)
Therefore, a man or even a woman who acts otherwise out of desire should be severely punished by the king; for by failing to restrain them, he becomes a sinner.
But when a quarrel arises between a husband and wife due to envy, malice, or passion, they should not dispute it before their kinsmen or the king. (Nar_12.89)

A child born of a man and woman who have abandoned each other and are mutually hostile shall be a Nāga; however, this is not the case for a woman who has committed adultery while her husband was away. (Nar_12.90)
In the event of infidelity, the woman shall undergo shaving of the head, sleeping on the ground, eating wretched food, wearing coarse clothing, and the labor of clearing away refuse.
A woman who has lost all her property through her husband's wealth, who causes an abortion,
or who desires the death of her husband, should be banished from the home.
A wise man should expel from his home that wife who is constantly inclined toward what is harmful, who speaks unpleasantly, and who eats before her husband.

One should not, out of desire, take pleasure in a barren woman, one who has given birth [only to daughters], one who is censurable, or one who is always hostile; by acting thus, he incurs fault. (Nar_12.94)
If a man abandons a wife who is compliant, not foul-mouthed, skillful, virtuous, and a mother of children, he shall be punished by the king with a heavy fine.

A woman who was married without her faults being known, who has departed and has not taken refuge with another, should be reinstated by her kinsmen; if she is without kinsmen, she should seek refuge on her own.
When her husband is lost, dead, has renounced the world, is impotent, or has fallen from his caste—
under these five calamities, another husband is ordained for women.
A Brāhmaṇa woman whose husband has gone abroad should wait for eight years if she is childless, but only four years if she has borne children; after that time, she may resort to another man.
A Kṣatriya woman who has not borne children may wait for six years; a Vaiśya woman who has borne children, for four years; but another (a Śūdra woman) shall live with him for two years. Nārada 12.99.
No specific time for cohabitation is prescribed for a Śūdra woman, nor is there any transgression of dharma;
however, if she has not borne a child, her stay [in the house] is limited to one year.
This law is prescribed for women whose husbands have gone abroad and do not return;
however, if the husband is heard to be alive, this rule shall be doubled.
This creation of living beings by Prajāpati occurred for the sake of the propagation of progeny;
thus, no such fault exists for women who go to another [man] in this manner.
The birth of castes in the direct order is known as *vidhi*;
that which occurs in the inverse order is to be understood as *varṇasaṃkara*. (Nar_12.103)

The son born of a woman one degree lower is known as the *anantara*; likewise, the son born of a woman two degrees lower is the *ekāntara*, and the son born of a woman three degrees lower is the *dvyantara*—both in the direct order (*anuloma*) and likewise in the inverse order (*pratiloma*).
The Ugra, the Pāraśava, and the Niṣāda are proclaimed as the three sons of Śūdra women born in the direct order from the three highest castes.
From a Brāhmaṇa woman as well, the Cāṇḍāla, the Sūta, and the Vaidehaka are born;
these three others are to be known as born in the inverse order (pratiloma) from the three [lower castes].
The Ambaṣṭha, the Māgadha, and the Kṣattṛ are the sons of Kṣatriya women;
among them, one is born in the direct order (ānulomya) and two are to be known as born in the inverse order (pratiloma).
The sons of a Vaiśya woman, however, are the Dauṣṣanta, Yavana, and Āyogava;
among these, one is born in the inverse order (prātilomya), while two are to be known as born in the natural order (anuloma).

Those born in the inverse order of castes, such as the Sūta and others, who are produced through the inverse order of birth, are the mixed castes (saṃkara), beginning with the Śvapāka; their group consists of twenty-one.
The son of a Brāhmaṇa from a wife of the same caste is a Savarṇa; from a Kṣatriya wife, he is an Anantara.
Likewise, the Ambaṣṭha and Ugra are the sons of a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya respectively. (Narada 12.110)
But the son of a Vaiśya woman from a Brāhmaṇa is the Dauṣṣanta, separated by one interval;
likewise, from a Kṣatriya and a Śūdra woman, one named Niṣāda is born.
A Śūdra woman bears a Pāraśava son from a Brāhmaṇa;
these are indeed proclaimed to be the sons born according to the natural order (ānulomya) of the castes.
The Sūta, the Māgadha, and likewise the Āyogava—these are the sons born from the castes in the reverse order; they are likewise considered "intermediate" (anantara).
The Sūta is declared to be the son born immediately after [the Kṣatriya], from a Brāhmaṇa woman by a Kṣatriya father;
likewise, the Māgadha and the Āyogava are the two sons of a Vaiśya and a Śūdra respectively.
A Brāhmaṇa woman bears to a Vaiśya a son called a Vaidehaka, who is one degree lower;
likewise, a Kṣatriya woman bears to a Śūdra a son called a Kṣattṛ, who is also one degree lower. (Nar_12.115)
When there is a confusion of castes through inverse union, the most wicked *cāṇḍāla* is born from a Śūdra father and a Brāhmaṇa mother who has fallen into delusion. (Nar_12.116)
The king must investigate so that no intermixture of castes occurs;
therefore, the king must especially protect the three Vedas from such confusion.
Where the partition of paternal property is carried out by the sons, that is declared by the wise to be the title of dispute known as "Inheritance" (dāyabhāga). (Narada 13.1)
When the father has died, the sons shall divide the father’s wealth;
in the absence of sons, the daughters; in their absence, the daughter’s offspring.
When his mother’s menses had ceased, when his sisters were married, and when his father had passed away, having cast off all desire for life; ||| Nar_13.3 |||
Or rather, the father himself, established in his final years, should divide the sons,
giving the eldest a superior share according as he deems fit.
The eldest brother should support all his younger brothers who desire it, just as a father does;
or a capable younger brother may do so, for in a family, religious rites depend upon one's ability.

Excluding the wealth acquired through valor and that obtained from a wife, as well as whatever may be the wealth acquired through learning— these three are indivisible, as is any gift received from a father.
And for one to whom his own mother has given her property out of affection, this same rule is seen to apply; for the mother is as beloved as the father. (Nar_13.7)
That which is received before the nuptial fire, that which is received as a dowry, and likewise the gift from the husband,
as well as what is received from brothers, the mother, and the father— this is declared to be the sixfold property of a woman.
The woman's property goes to her children; if she has no offspring, it goes to the husband.
However, in the case of the four [marriages] beginning with the Brāhma, they say it goes to the father; but in the others, it goes to the husband.
He who maintains the household of a brother who is acquiring knowledge shall receive a share from that wealth acquired through learning, even if he himself is unlearned. (Narada 13.10)

A physician shall not, against his will, give a share from his own wealth to one who is unlearned in medicine, unless that person relied upon the paternal estate and acquired it through him. (Narada 13.11)
When dividing his own property, a father shall take two shares for himself;
after her husband has died, the mother shall be entitled to an equal share with the sons. (Narada 13.12)
An additional share should be given to the eldest, for a special boon is ordained for the eldest;
the remaining brothers shall share equal portions, as shall an unmarried sister.
Likewise, among sons born of wives of lower castes according to the law, there is a gradual reduction in their shares when they are born of women who have been duly married. (Narada 13.14)
But for those who have been divided by their father with unequal shares of wealth— whether deficient, excessive, or equal—
that same rule shall apply to them, for the father is indeed the master of all.
The son born of an unmarried girl (kānīna), the son received with a bride (sahoḍha), and he who is born of a concealed woman (gūḍhaja)—
the man who marries them is to be known as their father, and they are declared to be heirs to a share of the estate.
He who is fatherless and born of an unmarried mother (kānīna) shall offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to his maternal grandfather and inherit his property.
Those who are born of an unauthorized woman—whether by one man or by many—are all non-inheritors;
they are the sons of the biological fathers alone.
If the mother was taken for a price, they shall offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to the biological father;
but if she was approached without a price, those offerings belong to the husband alone. (Narada 13.19)

One who hates his father, one who is outcasted, one who is impotent, and one who is born of adultery—even these sons of the body shall not receive a share; how much less so those born of the wife? (Narada 13.20)

Those in the family who are seized by long-lasting or severe illness, or who are dull-witted, insane, blind, or lame, must be maintained; however, their sons shall be entitled to a share of the inheritance.
Those who have two fathers (dvairāmuṣyāyaṇas) should offer the funeral cake and water separately to both;
likewise, they should take half a share from the inheritance for the benefit of both the progenitor and the owner of the field.
The share belonging to those who have lived together is ordained for them alone;
otherwise, among those without offspring, the heirs shall go to the others who are entitled to the shares.
If a brother should die without offspring, or if he should renounce the world,
his remaining brothers shall divide his wealth, excluding the woman's property.

They should provide for his maintenance until the end of their lives, provided they preserve the bed of their husband; however, if they do not, they may take back [the property] from the others. (Nar_13.25)
It may be that he who has a daughter is considered her father's heir for her maintenance;
until her marriage rites are performed, he should support her, but thereafter her husband shall maintain her.
When her husband has died, the husband’s kin are the masters of a woman who has no son;
they are the authority over her employment and protection, and they are the lords over her maintenance. (Narada Smṛti 13.27)
When the husband’s family has perished, being devoid of men and lacking support,
and even when his paternal kinsmen remain, it is the father’s side that is the authority over the woman.
At the conclusion of both [the husband's] life-stages, the king is declared to be the woman's protector;
he shall provide for her maintenance and restrain her if she deviates from the path. (Nar_13.29)
Even women born into noble families fall away through lack of independence;
therefore, Prajāpati ordained that they must not possess independence.
The father protects her in childhood, the husband protects her in youth, and the sons protect her in widowhood; a woman does not deserve independence. (Nar_13.31)
Whatever remains after the paternal inheritance has been given, as well as the father's debt, that must be divided by the brothers so that the father does not remain a debtor. (Narada 13.32)
And for those whose purificatory rites were not performed in due order by their father, these must be performed by their brothers from the paternal estate itself. (Narada 13.33)
If ancestral property is not available, the sacramental rites that must be performed should nevertheless be carried out by drawing from one's own share,
provided there are brothers who have already been consecrated.
He who is engaged in the affairs of the family and performs those duties should be supported by his brothers with food, clothing, and means of transport.

In cases of doubt regarding the law of partition, for the determination of the heirs' shares, and because of the separate performance of affairs by means of kinsmen and written records of division; Narada 13.36.
Among brothers who have not divided their inheritance, a single religious duty prevails;
once division has occurred, their religious duties shall also become separate for each.

The receipt of gifts, the ownership of cattle, food, houses, and fields, as well as cooking, religious duties, income, and expenditure, are to be understood as distinct for those who have been partitioned. (Narada 13.38)
Brothers who have divided their inheritance may act as witnesses, stand surety, give gifts, or receive them from one another; those who have not divided may not do so.
One should understand those persons among whose own heirs these transactions occur in the world to be divided, even in the absence of a written document. (Narada 13.40)
If many people are born of the same lineage, yet possess separate natures, separate activities,
and are endowed with separate qualities of action, they are not considered fit for joint undertakings.
If they should give their own shares, or even sell them, they may do all that as they wish; for they are masters of their own property. (Nar_13.42)

The legitimate son of the body, the son begotten on the wife, and the son of an appointed daughter, as well as the son of an unmarried girl, the son received with a bride, and likewise the son secretly born; Nar_13.43.
The son born again, the abandoned, the received, the purchased, the likewise made, and the one who has come of his own accord—these are declared to be the twelve kinds of sons. (Nar_13.44)
Among them, six are kinsmen and heirs, while six are kinsmen but not heirs;
each preceding one is considered superior, and each subsequent one is inferior.
For these [sons] would inherit that wealth after their father has died in due order; in the absence of each elder brother, the younger one shall obtain it. (Narada 13.46)
In the absence of a son, however, the daughter [is the heir], because she is seen to provide an equivalent lineage;
for both the son and the daughter are declared to be the perpetuators of the father's lineage.

In the absence of daughters, however, the kinsmen (sakulyas) and then the relatives (bāndhavas) [inherit]; after them, those of the same caste (sajātyas). In the absence of all these, it goes to the king.
Except for a Brahmin, however, a king devoted to righteousness should provide a livelihood for women; this is recorded as the rule for inheritance.
Whatever action is performed impulsively by those arrogant of their strength is called *sāhasa*; here, *saha* is said to mean strength. (Nar_14.1)

Furthermore, that [discipline] should be known as threefold—namely, the inferior, the middling, and the superior—and its specific characteristics have been explained separately in the treatises. (Nar_14.2)

The first degree of *sāhasa* (violence) is declared to consist of the breaking, throwing down, or crushing of fruits, roots, water, and other such items used for the cultivation of fields. (Narada 14.3)
Regarding clothing, livestock, food and drink, and household utensils—by this very same method, the middle amercement is prescribed. (Narada 14.4)
Malice, the use of poison or weapons, the violation of another's wife, and whatever else that deprives one of life— these are declared to be the highest form of violence (uttamasāhasa).
For the first of these, the punishment depends on the specific act and shall not be less than one hundred;
for the middle one, it should be known by those learned in the scriptures as being no less than five hundred.

Killing, confiscation of all property, banishment from the city, branding, and the amputation of limbs—these are declared to be the punishments for the highest degree of violence (uttamasāhasa). (Narada 14.7)
This rule of punishment is ordained for all without distinction;
except for execution, a Brāhmaṇa does not deserve death. (Narada 14.8)
Shaving the head is his punishment, as is banishment from the city;
moreover, he shall bear the mark of his crime upon his forehead and travel upon a donkey.
Those two may be fit for social intercourse if they have been punished for the first two [offenses];
however, even if punished, one who has committed the highest violence (uttamasāhasa) should be known as unfit for social intercourse.

Theft is a specific variety of that very same [taking what is not given], and its distinction is now stated: they call taking by force after an assault "extreme violence," whereas taking by deceit is "theft. (Narada 14.11)
That [gift] is also declared by the wise to be of three kinds, depending on the material:
namely, from the extraction of inferior, middling, or superior substances. (Nar_14.12)
Earthenware vessels, seats, beds, bones, wood, skins, grass, and the like, as well as pulses such as śamī and mung beans—these are declared to be minor items (kṣudradravya). (Nar_14.13)
Clothing, with the exception of silk; likewise cattle, with the exception of cows;
iron, with the exception of gold; and even rice and barley constitute the middling category.
Gold, jewels, silk garments, women, men, cattle, elephants, and horses,
as well as the property of gods, Brahmins, and kings, should be known as the highest category of wealth.
The wise declare that theft consists of the removal of these [goods] after deceiving them by various means, such as when they are asleep, careless, or intoxicated. (Nar_14.16)

Theft is established by the seizure of stolen goods; in the absence of such goods, it is established through the enjoyment [of the property]. Suspicion arises from association with wicked people, as well as from a lack of income and expenditure. (Narada 14.17)
Those who provide shelter to thieves as they move about, and those who,
though capable, look on with indifference, they too share in the guilt of that crime.
And those who, having heard the cries of people while their wealth is being carried off, do not run to the rescue, they too share in that fault. (Nar_14.19)
Whatever punishment has been prescribed by the wise for the three types of violent acts,
that same punishment applies to theft as well, according to the sequence of the three kinds of objects.
When cattle or other goods have been lost or stolen,
those who know the matter shall carry out the search by following the tracks until the source is reached.
In a village, a cow-pen, or a pasture, wherever the footprint should fall, it must be filled by that person; otherwise, he shall not lead it elsewhere. (Nar_14.22)
If his foot falters or breaks due to uneven ground near a village, he should cast it down there, where the nearest village or cattle-pen is located. (Naraka 14.23)

Likewise, where two [opposites] exist together in one place, by that very fact people are generally seen to be impure—either because of their past misdeeds or because they have associated with the wicked. (Nar_14.24)
Cāṇḍālas, executioners, and others who roam at night should conduct their searches within the villages, while those who travel abroad should conduct them outside.
If stones cannot be obtained, the king should provide them from his own wealth;
for by neglecting this, he becomes a sinner and falls away from both dharma and worldly prosperity.
Speech that is contrary in meaning, consisting of insults or slanders regarding one's country, birth, family, and so forth—that is called verbal cruelty (*vākpāruṣya*). (Nar_1516.1)
Because of its being harsh, abusive, or extreme, that [abuse] is also recorded as threefold;
according to the sequence of their gravity, the punishment here is also progressively heavier.

The wise say that speech accompanied by reproach and harshness is "indecorous" (aślīla), while that which is joined with the mention of physical defects and consists of insults leading to expulsion is called "severe" (tīvra).
Assaulting another’s body with hands, feet, weapons, and so forth,
or injuring them with ashes and the like, is called physical violence (*daṇḍapāruṣya*).
His [the king's] vision was also seen to be threefold— mild, moderate, and supreme— in sequence,
as indicated by his threatening gestures, his lack of hesitation, and the sight of his striking down [the enemy].

Because of the transgression involving inferior, middling, and superior objects, they say there are exactly three types of *sāhasa* (violent crimes); therein lies the purification of the thorns [of society].
The procedure for both of these has been stated as fivefold;
therein, purification and the liability to punishment are applied accordingly.
When harshness arises from agitation between two agitated parties,
he who forgives is considered the one who bears the burden, while he who transgresses is the one who suffers the penalty.
If no distinction were perceived between two people who are simultaneously engaged in the faults of harshness and being shrouded [by ignorance], then discipline would be the same for both.
He who first utters abuse will certainly be the one to bear the fault;
he who does so later is also an offender, yet for the former, discipline shall be more severe.
Furthermore, he who instigates two people who have both committed an offense incurs the punishment for them, whether it be the first or the other.
Toward dog-cookers, eunuchs, Caṇḍālas, and the deformed; toward those who live by killing, elephant-keepers, and the wives of outcasts; and toward the wives of one's preceptor and teacher.
When there is a transgression of the established rule, immediate execution itself is the punishment;
and the wise say that there is no fault in such severity of punishment.
For if these [officials] should overstep a virtuous person among men, that person alone should administer discipline; the king does not share in the responsibility for that lack of discipline.
For these are indeed stains among men; their wealth is of the nature of stain.
The king should have them executed, but he should not punish them with a fine.
A Kṣatriya who reviles a Brāhmaṇa deserves a fine of one hundred [paṇas];
a Vaiśya, one hundred and fifty or two hundred; but a Śūdra deserves corporal punishment.
A Brahmin should be fined fifty [paṇas] for defaming a Kṣatriya;
for a Vaiśya, the fine should be twenty-five; and for a Śūdra, the punishment shall be twelve.
For twice-born men of equal caste, the fine for transgression in disputes that are not worthy of discussion shall be exactly twelve; in such cases, it shall be double that amount.
If one speaks even truthfully of another who is one-eyed, lame, or otherwise similarly impaired, he shall be fined at least one kārṣāpaṇa by the king.
One should not, out of malice, defame one who has been purified according to the scriptures;
nor should one defame one who has been punished by the king, for he would incur the penalty for such transgression.
In this world, two are proclaimed to be beyond reproach and exempt from punishment:
the Brahmin and the king; for these two sustain this universe.
Having called one who has fallen a "fallen one," or a thief a "thief" again, one incurs an equal fault through such speech; if it be false, one incurs double the fault.
For a Śūdra who maliciously utters the names or castes of those [twice-born],
an iron spike eighteen finger-breadths long shall be driven into his body.
If he should arrogantly provide instruction in the Dharma to the twice-born,
the king shall cause heated oil to be poured into his mouth and his ears.
Whatever limb of a Brahmin by which he might commit an offense against a person of lower caste, that very limb of his shall be cut off; in this way, he may attain purification.

One born of a lower caste who seeks to sit on the same seat as one of superior caste shall be branded on the hip with the mark of a dog's foot and banished; or else, the king shall cause the region of his buttocks to be cut off.
If one spits out of arrogance, the king shall cause both lips to be cut off;
if one urinates upon him, his penis; and if one passes wind against him, his anus.
If someone seizes him by the hair, he should cut off both hands without hesitation;
likewise for seizing him by the feet, the nose, the neck, or the testicles.
But if one reviles a king who is established on his own path,
purification may come through the cutting off of the tongue or by the confiscation of all one's property.
That evil-minded person who would strike a king, even if the latter has committed an offense,
shall be cooked on a spit in fire for longer than the duration of a hundred murders of Brahmins.
A father does not incur punishment for the offense of his son, nor does a dog-owner for that of his dog,
nor does a monkey’s owner for that of his monkey— provided they were not sent by those very individuals.
Playing with dice, leather straps, or sticks, engaging in deceitful gambling, betting on animals, and similar contests constitute the practice known as *dyūta-samāhvaya*. (Nar_17.1)
The master of the gambling house shall conduct the game and receive what is owed for it;
his fee for conducting the gambling shall be ten percent of the winnings. (Narada 17.2)
When the dice fall twice in favor of the side on which a gambler has placed his stake, they say that victory belongs to the other player and defeat to that gambler. (Nar_17.3)
Gamblers should remain among gamblers when it comes to a dispute;
they alone shall be the observers of that matter, and they alone shall be the witnesses.
An impure gambler shall not resort to another gambling circle;
he shall not strike back at the master of the gaming house, nor shall he cause that man to pay his stake as he pleases.
One should expel from the gambling hall those wicked men who play with fraudulent dice;
having placed a rosary around their necks, for that is declared to be their disciplinary punishment. (Nar_17.6)
Furthermore, it should be known that the miscellaneous legal disputes (*prakīrṇaka*) concern matters relating to the king:
such as the defiance of the king's commands and likewise the failure to carry out his duties. (Narada 18.1)
The burning of cities, as well as the sowing of dissension among the subjects, and the subversion of the laws of heretics, guilds, corporations, and assemblies; Nar_18.2 //
Disputes between father and son, the transgression of penances, the neglect of receiving gifts, and even anger among those belonging to the stages of life (āśramas). Nar_18.3.
The fault of the intermixture of castes, as well as the restriction of their respective duties,
and whatever was not seen among the previous [codes], all that shall be found in the *Prakīrṇaka*.
But the king, being attentive, should protect all the stages of life by means of the four expedients prescribed in the treatises as well as those inherent to them.
Whichever caste should decline, or whichever should attain excellence—seeing that very one fallen from its own path, one should establish it upon the right way. (Nar_18.6)
And regarding other acts not prescribed by the scriptures that are joined with sin,
the king, having carefully considered his own capacity, shall inflict punishment upon those deserving of punishment.
The king should not promote that which is contrary to the Śruti and Smṛti and detrimental to the people, nor should he allow it to continue once it has been set in motion. (Nar_18.8)

Whatever has been done by another king that is devoid of justice, or whatever has been done through ignorance—that too, being established unjustly, he should bring back into accordance with justice. (Nar_18.9)
That man who does not observe the laws promulgated by the king is a sinner who should be punished; he who violates the royal decree deserves death. (Nar_18.10)
The weapons of those who live by arms, the draft animals of those who live by beasts of burden, the ornaments of courtesans, and the musical instruments of those skilled in them; Nar_18.11.
Whatever is the tool of anyone, by which artisans live their lives—the king ought not to seize these even when confiscating all one's property. (Nar 18.12)
He is without beginning and without end, the lord of the earth among bipeds;
for if he had not strayed from the path, he would be radiant and pure.
If the king did not administer punishment to all the social classes who have strayed from the path, these subjects would perish. (Nar_18.14)
A Brahmin may abandon his status as a Brahmin, and a Kshatriya may relinquish his kshatriya duties;
a Vaishya may abandon his own work, but a Shudra should distinguish himself in all respects. (Nar_18.15)
If there were no kings on earth to wield the rod of punishment, the stronger would roast the weaker like fish on a spit. (Nar_18.16)
The constant favoring of the virtuous and likewise the restraint of the wicked—this is remembered as the duty of kings, and their purpose is achieved by the subduing of enemies. (Nar_18.17)
Just as fire, while constantly burning these creatures, is not defiled, so too a king, while inflicting punishment upon those deserving of it, is not defiled. (Nar_18.18)
The authority of kings is their majesty, and that is established in their speech;
whatever they may say, whether it be false or true, that is the law for those engaged in legal proceedings.
This one called a king moves upon the earth as the thousand-eyed Indra in person;
the subjects should never remain anywhere in defiance of his command.

Because he holds the office of protection, because of his lordship, and because he is seen to favor living beings, whatever the king ordains is authoritative; such is the established rule. (Nar_18.21)
Just as a husband is always worthy of honor by women even if he lacks virtues,
so too is a lord of men worthy of honor by his subjects even if he is devoid of merit.
Subjects are purchased by the king through his asceticism; therefore, the monarch is their master.
Consequently, one must abide by his word, and their livelihood is dependent upon him.
Kings of immeasurable power bear five forms:
those of Agni, Indra, Soma, Yama, and Dhanada.
When a ruler, having fallen under the sway of anger for some reason or even without cause, consumes his subjects, he is then called "fire. (Nar_18.25)
When a king, desiring victory, takes up his weapons and advances against his enemies by relying upon fiery energy, he is then declared to be Indra.
When the king, free from the heat of anger and appearing joyful, goes to see his subjects, he is then called Soma. (Nar_18.27)
When the illustrious king, seated upon the throne of Dharma, wields the rod of punishment with impartiality toward all beings, he is then Yama, the son of Vivasvat.
But when a lord of the earth favors supplicants, elders, the wise, servants,
and others with gifts, then he is considered a giver of wealth (Dhanada).
Therefore, one should not despise him, nor revile him, nor treat him with contempt;
one should abide by his command, for death would result from its transgression. (Nar_18.30)
His duty consists of protecting the subjects, serving the elderly and the wise, presiding over legal proceedings, and guarding himself. (Nar_18.31)
A king, with a concentrated mind, should constantly attend upon the Brahmins;
for the Kṣatriya power joined with the Brahmins is the root of the protection of the world. (Nar_18.32)
A Brahmin is exempt from the obligation [of rising], yet he must sit before a Kṣatriya;
he is the first to be seen in the morning and must offer salutations to all. (Nar_18.33)
The first-fruits of the new harvest and the right of way for those traveling were his;
furthermore, his entry into the houses of others for the sake of alms was unimpeded. (Nar_18.34)
One should practice non-stealing regarding the gathering of firewood, flowers, and water from what is possessed by others;
one should not make demands upon others, nor engage in conversation with the wives of others.
On rivers, he may cross without paying a ferry fee, as may those who have already crossed; likewise, he need not pay tolls at ferries, provided that crossing is not his primary means of trade.
A Brahmin traveling on the road, exhausted, taking for himself two stalks of sugarcane and five radishes while staying nowhere, commits no offense. (Nar_18.37)
One should not accept [a gift] from those who are accused, nor from the fallen, nor from enemies, nor from atheists;
nor from one who uses deception, nor for no reason, nor by afflicting the donor.
Because of the great variety of objects and because they are given by high-souled beings,
receiving gifts from kings is superior [to receiving them] from others, with the exception of Brahmins.
Both the brahmin and the king are observers of firm vows; there is no difference between them, for both are devoted to the protection of the subjects and the dharma. (Nar_18.40)
They say that even for a sharp-witted lord of the earth who knows the Dharma, is grateful, and rules over the impure for the sake of protection, his wealth is indeed pure.
Just as the confluence of pure and impure waters attains equality within the ocean, so too does the influx of wealth to a king. (Nar_18.42)
Just as gold placed in a blazing fire attains purity,
even so do all the scriptures attain their purification through kings.
Whoever gives their own property to Brahmins, that should be permitted by the king as well; this is the eternal dharma.
From whatever other appropriate land is designated as one-sixth [of the produce],
that tribute is ordained for him as his wages for protecting the subjects.
That which has been made over to one who is not a Brahmin can be taken back;
but that which has been given to a Brahmin cannot be seized again. (Nar_18.46)

Giving, study, and sacrifice—these are his three types of ritual action; officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and receiving gifts constitute his means of livelihood, the third being the acceptance of gifts. (Nar_18.47)

A twice-born man should remain established in his own duty and maintain a livelihood earned through lawful means; he should not accept gifts from the unworthy among the social classes when they lack self-restraint.
How is it that the king is not a deity—he by whose word an impure man becomes pure, and a pure man instantly becomes impure? (Nar_18.49)
O Vidura, those twice-born ones who accept the gifts of that king of immeasurable splendor, knowing him to be truly divine, are not defiled.
In this world, there are eight auspicious things: a Brahmin, a cow, fire, gold, clarified butter, the sun, water, and likewise, a king as the eighth.
One should constantly behold these, pay homage to them, and worship them;
one should also circumambulate them, for in this way one's lifespan is not diminished. (Nar 18.52)
The supplement:
It should be known that there are two kinds of thieves who seize the property of others—the open and the secret; a self-possessed king should recognize them as such. (Nar_19.1)
There were deceivers who used false measures and scales,
extortionists, violent men, gamblers, and courtesans.
Those who produce counterfeits and those whose livelihood depends on auspicious signs—such as these should be known as deceivers of the light of the world. (Nar 19.3)
They should be known as unmanifest, residing both outside and within;
they rob men by overpowering them while they are asleep or heedless.
Those who destroy districts, villages, and houses; those who obstruct paths; pickpockets;
and others such as these are to be known as secret thieves.
Having learned of them, those well-skilled spies who perform such duties should follow and seize them by means of men stationed in secret.
Assembly halls, water-stations, bakeries, brothels, taverns, and food-sellers; crossroads, sacred trees, public gatherings, and spectacles—Nar_19.7.
These empty houses, forests, and shrines for deities must be patrolled by those intent on capturing thieves.
In the same way, others who are appointed as trustworthy and eloquent speakers—
spies indeed— would incite those thieves, just as former thieves did.
They should bring about their meeting by means of gifts of food and drink, by attending social gatherings and festivals, and likewise under the pretext of theft.
Those who do not approach there, even though they have been sent and dispatched,
must be pursued and captured along with their sons, cattle, and kinsmen.
Whichever thieves he might capture there, having beaten and humiliated them,
and having proclaimed it everywhere, they were to be executed by various forms of capital punishment.
For thieves who have not been caught in the act and do not confess shall be executed by the king;
however, those caught in the act along with their tools, the king should swiftly punish as thieves.
Those who would strike at their own country, as well as those who obstruct the highways—having confiscated all their property, one should further subject them to censure. (Nar_19.14)
One should interrogate those caught as thieves on suspicion of being *ahoḍha* (robbers);
by means of various threats and stratagems, they shall speak exactly as it was done.
The place, the time, the direction, the caste, the name, or the dwelling;
the task, and who the laborers may be—these are the things that should be inquired about when suppressing [the enemy].
Because of differences in complexion, voice, and appearance; because of reporting with uncertainty;
because of being seen at an improper place and time; and because of not having purified even one's clothing. (Nar_19.17)

One should ascertain [the guilt] even by slight signs—due to the expenditure of what is not one's own, prior acts of theft, and association with evildoers—and not solely by the seizure of stolen goods. (Narada 19.18)

If there should be suspicion against a man who follows the way of a bandit, or even against a thief, and if he should be touched by even a slight [taint], then an ordeal must be performed. (Nar_19.19)

Those who provide food for thieves, as well as those who give them fire and water, those who grant them shelter, those who act as their guides, and likewise those who provide them with provisions; // Nar_19.20 //
Those who purchase goods, those who receive them as gifts, and those who conceal them—all these are declared by the law to be subject to equal punishment. (Narada 19.21)
Those appointed as provincial governors and the feudal lords within the realms who remain neutral during times of attack are exactly like thieves. (Nar_19.22)
If a thief should plunder within the range of someone's property, that person must diligently search for the thieves;
otherwise, he shall be made to pay for the theft, provided the tracks have not departed.
But when that footprint has vanished, been lost, or fallen elsewhere,
one should cause the neighboring kings, the guardians of the roads, and the guardians of the quarters to be made to pay.
If a house has indeed been robbed, the king shall cause the thieves to be seized from the guards and the provincial officials, provided that the thief is not apprehended. (Narada 19.25)
Or, if there is doubt regarding those being compelled to pay in that theft,
the one who claims to have been robbed shall be made to swear an oath for the sake of clearing himself of the charge of theft.
If a non-thief is made to pay a fine on the grounds that he is being cleared of the charge of theft,
they shall, upon the actual thief being found, be made to pay double what was paid.
One should diligently restore an item stolen by thieves in its original form;
in the absence of that, its value shall be paid, and a fine equal to that amount must be imposed.
Of pieces of wood, stalks, grass, and the like, as well as those made of clay;
of bamboo and vessels made of bamboo, and of cane, sinew, bone, and leather.
In the case of stealing vegetables, greens, and roots, as well as fruits and flowers, products of cow's milk, sugarcane derivatives, and likewise salt and oil; Nar_19.30 //
For cooked grains, prepared foods, intoxicants, and meat—all those of low value—the fine shall be five times their price. (Narada 19.31)
For all goods measured by weight,
by measure, or by number, as well as for those of superior value among these, the fine shall be ten times their value.
Manu declared that for one who steals more than ten jars of grain, the punishment is death; however, for stealing less than that, he should be made to pay a fine eleven times the value.
For stealing more than a hundred of gold, silver, and the like, as well as excellent garments and the finest gems, the punishment is death. (Nar_19.34)
For one who abducts a man, the punishment is the highest amercement;
for one who abducts a woman, the forfeiture of all property; but for one who abducts a maiden, the penalty is death.

For one who steals large animals, the punishment is the highest amercement; for stealing a medium-sized animal, the middle amercement; and for stealing a small animal, the first amercement. (Narada 19.36)
The first [type] has a minimum of twenty-four [verses], while the latter consists of ninety-six;
the middle type consists of five hundred verses, with two hundred as its minimum.
A fine of one thousand is to be known as the highest, while that of five hundred is the lowest;
thus has the threefold punishment for violent crimes been proclaimed by the Self-Existent One.
In the first case of breaking a knot, there shall be the cutting off of the fingers and the thumb;
in the second case, the rest of that [limb] shall be cut off, along with the first amercement.
For cutting the udder of cows belonging to Brahmins, there shall be the amputation of a large portion;
but for one who steals a female slave, there shall always be the amputation of half a foot.
"By whatever specific limb a thief acts out his offense, that very limb of his must be cut off; such is the instruction of Manu. (Nar_19.41)
Whether the offense is against one of higher status or against one who is not of higher status,
one should inflict a heavier punishment on a thief than what is prescribed for a first-time offender.
The self-existent Manu has declared ten places for punishment, which apply to the three social classes; the Brāhmaṇa is always to be protected from them.
The genitals, the belly, the tongue, the hands, and the feet as the fifth;
the eyes, the nose, the ears, wealth, and likewise the body.
Having fully understood the offense, as well as the place and time in their true nature, and having considered the essential strength and the consequences, he should prescribe these punishments.
A king must not release a perpetrator of violence for the sake of a friend or because of the acquisition of vast wealth; such a person has abandoned his own life, as Manu has declared. (Nar_19.46)

As much demerit accrues to a king from the execution of one who should not be executed, so much does he incur from releasing one who deserves to be executed; yet for him who restrains the wicked, there is merit.
One must never kill a brahmin, even if he is established in every kind of evil; one may, at will, banish him—thus is the dharma established. (Nar_19.48)
The king may seize all his property, or he may leave a fourth part remaining;
remembering the duty toward his dependents, he should follow the law of Prajāpati—this is the established rule.
But for a Brahmin’s offense, branding on four limbs is prescribed:
for violating the Guru’s bed, for drinking liquor, for theft, and for harming a Brahmin. (Narada 19.50)
For violating the teacher's bed, the mark of a female organ should be made; for drinking liquor, a flag is prescribed;
for theft, having made the footprint of a dog, one should brand it with the bile of a peacock.
The forehead of the killer of a fetus must be branded with the mark of a headless corpse;
furthermore, he must be made unfit for social intercourse—this is the instruction of Manu.
The thief must go before the king with disheveled hair, running and confessing that theft, saying: "I have done this; punish me. (Nar_19.53)
By this act, he becomes a thief because he has carried out his own deed;
that guilt shall touch the king who releases him while he is still defiled by sin.
But those men who have committed sins and have been punished by kings go to heaven stainless, just like virtuous people who have performed good deeds.
Whether through punishment or through release, the thief is freed from his guilt;
however, by failing to punish him, the king incurs the guilt of that thief. (Nar_19.56)
The teacher is the instructor for those who possess self-control; the king is the instructor for the wicked;
but for those whose sins are concealed, Yama, the son of Vivasvat, is the instructor.
The guilt for theft incurred by a Śūdra is eightfold;
that of a Vaiśya is twice eightfold, and that of a Kṣatriya is thirty-twofold.
"Sixty-four [years] for a Brāhmaṇa"—thus Svāyambhuva has declared;
and even therein, it should be especially greater among those who are learned. (Nar_19.59)
Punishment is traditionally held to be of two kinds: corporal and monetary.
Corporal punishments are said to be tenfold, while monetary punishments are manifold.
The monetary fine begins with a *kākaṇī* and likewise ends with the confiscation of all one's property;
the corporal punishment begins with confinement and likewise ends with the taking of life. (Narada 19.61)
The punishment beginning with a *kākaṇī* is traditionally held to culminate in a *māṣa*;
that which was declared to begin with a *māṣa* culminates in a *kārṣāpaṇa*. (Narada 19.62)
But for offenses beginning with a *kārṣāpaṇa* and ending with four *kārṣāpaṇas*, another [fine] begins with two and ends with eight; and another begins with three and ends with twelve.
All those [fines] beginning with the *kārṣāpaṇa* that have been mentioned should each be multiplied by four; other [fines] should be understood in the same way, up to the first *sāhasa*. 19.64.
In the southern direction, the silver kārṣāpaṇa circulates;
in the eastern direction, it is fixed at sixteen paṇas. (Nar_19.65)
A *māṣa* should be known as one-twentieth of a *kārṣāpaṇa*;
a *kākaṇī*, however, is one-fourth of both a *māṣa* and a *paṇa*.
In the region of the Five Rivers, however, there is a conventional designation;
by that [designation], the measure of a *kārṣāpaṇa* is indeed fixed here.
A *kārṣāpaṇa* should be known as equal to four *aṇḍikās*, and four of those make one *dhānaka*.
Twelve of those [make] a *suvarṇa*; a *dīnāra* is recorded as being the same as a *citraka*.
