The king should constantly follow the threefold Vārttā, the Trayī, and the science of government (Daṇḍanīti) with unflagging vigilance;
he should eliminate those caught in his realm by skillful means and suppress the wicked within both the city and the countryside.
When no witness is available in a dispute among litigating men,
then one should examine them by means of ordeals and various kinds of oaths.
Truth, vehicles, weapons, cattle, seeds, and silver;
the ancestors, the gods, and one's own feet—these have been given as well as meritorious deeds.
In cases of great offense, the lord of the earth should cause divine ordeals to be administered;
but for minor matters, O best of men, he should cause the man to swear by oaths.
For these oaths have been declared as easy to perform when the doubt is slight;
however, in cases of violence and formal accusation, the procedure for divine proof (divya) is proclaimed.
"Regarding a matter in doubt, and especially concerning those who have concealed [their actions], the divine ordeal is to be known as fivefold; so said the blessed Manu. (Narada 20.5)
The balance, fire, water, poison, and the fifth, the sacred libation—
these are declared to be the ordeals for the purification of those who are accused.
For the sake of purifying those accused in doubtful cases, the high-souled Nārada further proclaimed these methods for discerning truth from falsehood;
a wise man should cause the trial to proceed with the consent of the litigant, and not otherwise.
The two pillars of the balance are proclaimed to be four cubits in height;
their measurement in circumference is seen to be six cubits. (Nar_20.8)
The distance between the two feet should be one cubit and a half;
having suspended two scales upon the sturdy crocodile-shaped beam of the balance, Narada 20.9.
Having first weighed the man, one should mark the balance; then, having lowered him from the balance so that he is equalized with the empty arm of the scale, [one should proceed]. (Nar_20.10)
Having secured him with the ritual pledges (samaya), the man should mount [the wheel] once more;
when this has been done, if she remains perfectly motionless while being held against his side, [he succeeds].
If, when weighed, he increases [in weight], he is pure; of this there is no doubt.
But if he remains equal or decreases, the man would not be pure.
By the words of this legal discourse, you are called the "Balance" (Dhaṭa).
You know the sins and the good deeds of all living beings;
O Balance, you alone know those things which human beings do not perceive.
This man, accused in a legal dispute, is being weighed in that very manner;
you ought to save him from his state of uncertainty according to the Dharma.
Henceforth, I shall explain the supreme procedure for the metal [test]:
the distance from one circle to the next circle is thirty-two finger-breadths.
Thus, by means of eight circles, two hundred and twenty-four finger-breadths are declared by those who perceive the true meaning of the principles of enumeration. (Nar_20.16)
Having thus dwelt within the imagined mandalas, even though he is pure,
he should wrap seven *aśvattha* leaves with a thread around his two hands.
One should take a ball of heated iron weighing fifty palas with both hands and walk slowly seven steps.
One should not step beyond the mandala, nor should one set foot within it; and one should not let the foot fall before reaching the ground that has been prepared. (Nar_20.19)
Having crossed over by means of this procedure while remaining composed, that man who is unburned on all sides shall become purified. (Nar_20.20)

If one who has not been burnt casts down [the balance] out of fear, or if he is found to be trembling, one should cause him to carry the iron again; this is the ancient rule. By this procedure, the ordeal by fire is prescribed.
O Agni, you move within all living beings like a witness;
there is no good deed or evil deed in the world that remains unknown to you. (Nar_20.22)
You know exactly as they are the hidden misdeeds and good deeds of men—those which human beings themselves do not perceive. (Nar_20.23)
"This man has been accused in a legal dispute and desires purification; therefore, you ought to rescue him from this state of uncertainty in accordance with dharma. (Nar_20.24)
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the supreme ritual for the water:
one should discharge three arrows with a bow that is not excessively cruel. (Nar_20.25)
But a man of lesser age should take up the middle arrow;
then, once it has been brought back, that man shall be purified.
Otherwise, he would not be pure; he might reveal even a single limb, or move from his place to another where he had previously been stationed. (Nar_20.27)
Women should not be forced by force, nor should even a weak man;

because of their timidity, death may overcome a woman, and force may overcome even one who is emaciated. One might suddenly incur all [these misfortunes]; therefore, one should not submerge them. (Nar_20.28)
In the midst of the water, he firmly grasped the man's thighs with great restraint.
Regarding the distinction between truth and falsehood, water and fire are the most effective means of clarification;
since fire arose from this [water], therefore water is superior.

The purification of those who have been defiled is performed by those who know the true nature of reality; therefore, O Blessed One, Lord of Waters, you ought to save us through the power of truth. (Nar_20.31)
Henceforth I shall proclaim the supreme procedure for poison:
having first weighed the poison, this should be administered at the onset of winter.
One who knows the Dharma should not cause [the gift] to be given in the forenoon, nor at midday, nor at twilight;
nor during the autumn, summer, spring, or the rainy season. (Nar_20.33)
One should carefully avoid *kālakūṭa* and *alaṃbu* poisons, as well as those that are broken, split, fumigated, or mixed. (Nar_20.34)

The Śārṅga stone from the Himalayas is highly recommended; endowed with excellent fragrance, color, and taste, it should be given by a king who desires to know the truth to one who possesses great faults. (Nar_20.35)

One should not administer [the ordeal] to children, the sick, or the elderly, nor to those who have committed only a very minor offense; however, for one to be cleared of a charge, one should cause them to swallow seven barley-grains soaked in clarified butter.
From six *pala*s of poison, one should take that portion which is the twentieth part;
having reduced that by one-eighth, one should administer it soaked in clarified butter (*ghṛta*) to the person to be cleared of suspicion.
Having touched the Brahmins according to the prescribed rite and being permitted by them,
he, while fasting, should eat in the presence of the gods and the Brahmins.
If the poison is digested easily, free from violent onset and exhaustion, the king, recognizing it as pure, should honor and release him. (Nar_20.39)
O Poison, you are the son of Brahmā, established in devotion to truth and dharma;
purify this man from sin, and by means of his truth, become nectar for him. Nar_20.40.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the supreme rule for the treasury. 20.41.
In the forenoon, for one who has fasted, bathed, and is wearing wet clothes,
who possesses a beard and is free from vices, the drinking of the ordeal liquid (kośapāna) is prescribed.

Whichever deity a person is devoted to, one should have that person consume an offering dedicated to that deity. Whatever personal symptom appears after seven days or again after fourteen days, that itself is the manifestation of his [guilt]. 20.43.
If, after two weeks have passed, a person suffers a grave disorder,
they should not be accused by the learned, because the appointed time has elapsed.

One should avoid the ordeal of drinking from the sacred vessel (*kośapāna*) in the case of those who have committed a great offense, those devoid of dharma, the ungrateful, the impotent, the contemptible, atheists, outcasts (*vrātya*), and slaves. (Nar_20.45)
In the manner described, the king who knows the Dharma should administer the five ordeals to those accused; he rejoices both in this world and after death.
One should not give poison to a Brāhmaṇa; a Kṣatriya should not take away gold;
a Vaiśya should not immerse himself in water; and one should not have a Śūdra drink from the royal treasury.
One should not administer poison during the rains; one should not cause [the accused] to drown in water during the winter;
one should not have him swallow molten metal in the summer; nor should one have him drink from the divine vessel (kośa) at night.
The Nāradīya Dharmaśāstra is completed.
